  some would think its bullsh when they hear that writing can declutter one's mind, but please do it first. don't even try to make it pretty. i've the ugliest handwriting and idc but that what makes me keep going. i stopped trying hard to make it look pretty as i used to back then which clearly didn't work for me for many reasons hence why i quit. 
  
  i can't say much about other things but what i can say is it definitely helps you to think more clearly, if you're really honest in your writing. 
  
  just start with anything. even just 5 words today? do it.

      Your memory is like a cup; too much information can make it overflow. Don't binge videos. Take time to take in information, like you would with high quality food. The more your brain works over a subject, the more likely it is to retain elements. Learn what distracts you, or ways you learn better... Change things up and try other methods! In the end, you'll get more confident on how YOU learn - that's the important part. I have attention deficit and I can vouch that anyone can learn! I've been behind all my life  and let me tell you that you need to be kind and gentle with yourself, or your brain will just block everything. Try to hanging out with people who are kind and supportive - they won't make you feel like you're behind =)
    ↳ **@Floyd..B** (👍7 · 2026-02-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6nvyilkTF0&lc=Ugz6Xjel1pvDFxXR-Lt4AaABAg.ASkd-l2HUFEASlnlARMGEw
      Here is some advice from me (I had the same problems) :
      
      - Get some sleep, at least about 8H every night, this is very important, quality of sleep is too. You should also go to bed at regular hours.
      - Eat high quality, unprocessed food, don't worry about cholesterol (a bit of cholesterol is good for the brain), just avoid too much fat and reduce sugar (do it gradually to avoid problems).
      - Drink plenty of mineral water.
      - Get some exercise ! Lift heavy weights and do some cardio training. When bored, or stuck in your work, go for a 15 min walk.
      
      It may seem simple, but this is what helped me so much.

**@DCAcuity** (👍5 · 2026-04-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y89OLiozqNY&lc=Ugyk2ZR0iXZIWTdec0Z4AaABAg
  Nah, James is much more than just an English teacher. What he’s really teaching is a form of human development — how to think and learn without the discouragement that comes from the “perfect score” mentality many of us were trained into as kids.
  
  This is something I’ve started to recognize as I’ve gained more education in a field. In the past, I would say someone wasn’t a great teacher (and sometimes that was true) but another problem was that I wasn’t actually reading with the right mindset. I was reading just to complete the assignment, to encode information and move on. I wasn’t stepping back to ask what the author was actually trying to communicate.
  
  That’s why reading research papers always felt easier to me. The entire STRUCTURE of research is built around an argument. The abstract basically says: “Most of the literature says X, but here is why I think Y is more accurate, and here is the method and evidence supporting that claim.” Then the discussion section places the findings back into conversation with the broader literature — what psychology sometimes calls the “Other,” meaning the internalized body of perspectives and prior work that the author is responding to, critiquing, or refining.
  
  After watching a couple of James’s videos — where he broke down ideas I had previously encountered in learning psychology into more practical, active examples — it finally clicked for me: almost everything you read is structured around a point. There is always a main idea, an argument, or a claim the author is trying to communicate. Once that clicked, it also explained something about my undergraduate experience. “Boring” readings felt paralyzing because I didn’t see a reason to engage with them. If I wasn’t interested, there was no clear “why” for reading, so my brain treated the text like meaningless information to push through. Without a perceived point, the motivation just wasn’t there.
  
  Now the approach is different. Even if the material is dry, I read with a simple goal: figure out what the author is trying to say. Once you frame everything as someone making a point, whether it’s an argument, explanation, or interpretation, the reading process becomes much faster and clearer. You’re not just absorbing words anymore; you’re tracing a line of thought.
  
  Note: Note: I was still able to perform exceptionally well in undergrad despite this. I’m now in graduate school and continuing to do well, and I’ve had the opportunity to contribute to research across several areas — mathematics, law, machine learning, and counseling psychology. Those are simply subjects that interest me. What I’ve come to realize, though, is that purpose is the foundation of motivation, especially once raw necessity is no longer driving you. I come from very little, so early on survival and obligation provided the motivation. Once that pressure fades, motivation can feel like a vacuum if you don’t have a clear sense of purpose behind what you’re doing. What changed for me is recognizing that I can engage with almost any subject when I frame it as purposeful communication. Once I’m trying to understand what someone is actually trying to say and why, the material becomes far easier to work through. Looking back, I realize this was really a gap in my metacognition. I didn’t fully grasp the mental process behind how I was reading and processing information. What’s interesting is that even many researchers don’t articulate this process as operationally or clearly as James has in his recent videos.
  
  Look at James man, blessing a generation. May Christ bless you sir.

      It's a good thing you added Turkish to the translations; following along with the subtitles is as important as listening (more effective than the movie).
      
      When I was a kid, even though I didn't have any foreign language speakers around me (still don't), I could distinguish many languages, especially Italian and Spanish (we had a radio that picked up foreign radio frequencies, but (as much as you can listen to 🙄)). Despite not having any musicians around me, I could recognize almost all instruments by their sound and appearance.
      
      Today, these things don't seem so familiar.
      
      How do you interpret this as an educator?
      
      As the saying goes;
      "All foreign languages, including them, are already stored in the human brain as data..."
      
      Empathy may not be as good as it seems; to understand this, we have to hit rock bottom; You'll understand when you see how much effort you put into teaching others.
      
      Did you gain weight like me, or did you do too much weight training? 🙄
      
      Hello to all teachers, each of our classes are enjoyable and informative.🌼🖐️🌼
    ↳ **@NihalTÜRK-u7b** (👍0 · 2025-12-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RgjUjpAyB2M&lc=Ugwh9KcGds_hhfJx1vh4AaABAg.APtqFsZVch5APvBhZtxaVq
      C'est une bonne chose que vous ayez ajouté le turc aux traductions ; suivre les sous-titres est aussi important qu'écouter (et même plus efficace que le film).
      
      Quand j'étais enfant, même si je n'avais pas de locuteurs étrangers autour de moi (et ce n'est toujours pas le cas), je distinguais beaucoup de langues, surtout l'italien et l'espagnol (nous avions une radio qui captait les fréquences étrangères, mais bon, on ne peut pas vraiment les écouter 🙄). Bien que je n'aie jamais entendu de musiciens, je reconnaissais presque tous les instruments à leur son et à leur apparence.
      
      Aujourd'hui, ces choses me semblent bien moins naturelles.
      
      Comment interprétez-vous cela en tant qu'enseignant ?
      
      Comme le dit l'adage :
      
      « Toutes les langues étrangères, y compris celles-ci, sont déjà stockées dans le cerveau humain sous forme de données… »
      
      L'empathie n'est peut-être pas aussi efficace qu'on le croit ; pour le comprendre, il faut toucher le fond. Vous comprendrez quand vous verrez tous les efforts que vous déployez pour enseigner aux autres.
      
      Avez-vous pris du poids comme moi, ou avez-vous fait trop de musculation ? 🙄
      
      Bonjour à tous les professeurs ! Nos cours sont tous agréables et instructifs. 🌼🖐️🌼

      В детстве, несмотря на то, что рядом не было носителей иностранных языков (и сейчас их нет), я различал много языков, особенно итальянский и испанский (у нас был радиоприёмник, который ловил иностранные частоты, но (насколько можно слушать 🙄)).   This is what I learned from this video, thanks James ❤
  
  1. We must have a vision, why we are going to do that stuff? Imagine yourself as a big version a better version or a better world, this is useful to project what we want to be or what we want to improve.
  2. We must practice. If we have a big vision, we cannot hope that we're going to achieve it right now, because Fear is the mind killer. So when we see an overwhelming amount of things that we have to do, that is counter-productive, because we discourage ourselves to start doing them. Thus, How we are going to do that stuff? Well, don't scary your amygdala, since amygdala manage your fear, so we must have to ask little questions What could I do to be better than yesterday, take short steps don't rush your goals, since the amygdala will be scary.
  3. We must execute, what we are going to do to reach that goal? We started having a vision, then we knew that we have to take small steps don't rush, so now we have to make a plan about what to do, this is feasible using the 12 weeks method. That is dividing the year into 4 parts of 12 weeks which are separate stages, so we focus deeply on the different parts that we divided before to improve constantly and at the end of the stages we have done a lot of progress in our goals.
  
  I'm still acquiring English, so I'm open for any feedback, thank your for reading.

  This video dives into how reading can dramatically boost your English fluency. James explains several cognitive processes involved in reading:
  - Saccades: Quick eye movements that help you scan text.
  - Smooth pursuit: Tracking words as you read, which improves focus.
  - Subvocalization: The habit of silently pronouncing words in your mind — useful but can slow you down.
  - Sustained reading: Maintaining attention over longer texts to build comprehension and stamina.

  •the subject can see the pain in the other person and feels sorry for them. 
  Empathy 
  •to experience the emotions of another person. 
  Apethy-away from emotions 
  Imply
  • to say smth indirectly. 
  Infer
  • come to a conclusion from the evidence or thinking with information.

      English Conversation topic: Dining Out with Friends
      
      1. Planning to Dine Out:
      
      "Hey, do you want to grab dinner together this weekend?"
      "I'm craving [type of cuisine]. Would you be interested in trying that restaurant with me?"
      "Let's go out for dinner to celebrate [occasion]."
      "I heard about this new restaurant downtown. Do you want to check it out with me?"
      "I'm in the mood for some good food and company. Who's up for dinner tonight?"
      
      2. Making Plans:
      
      "Sounds like a plan! What time should we meet?"
      "Count me in! Where are we meeting?"
      "I'm down for dinner. Which restaurant did you have in mind?"
      "I'm free after 7 PM. Does that work for everyone?"
      "Great! Let's make a reservation to avoid waiting too long."
      
      3. Choosing a Restaurant:
      
      "Do you have any preferences for cuisine, or are you open to suggestions?"
      "I'm in the mood for Italian food. How does that sound?"
      "Is there a particular restaurant you've been wanting to try?"
      "I know a great sushi place nearby. Would you be interested?"
      "Let's find a place that accommodates everyone's dietary preferences."
      
      4. Ordering Food:
      
      "I think I'll start with the [appetizer]. What about you?"
      "Everything on the menu looks delicious. I'm having a hard time deciding!"
      "I'm going to try the [dish]. Has anyone had it before?"
      "I'm allergic to [ingredient], so I'll need to make sure it's not in my dish."
      "Let's share some dishes family-style so we can try a little bit of everything."
      
      5. Enjoying the Meal:
      
      "This [dish] is amazing! I'm glad I ordered it."
      "I've never tried [ingredient] before. It's actually really good!"
      "The presentation of these dishes is so impressive."
      "The flavors in this dish are so well-balanced."
      "I'm really enjoying the atmosphere of this restaurant."
      
      6. Conversation Topics:
      
      "So, what's everyone been up to lately?"
      "Have you seen any good movies or TV shows recently?"
      "Did anyone hear about [current event]? What are your thoughts on it?"
      "Let's reminisce about some of our favorite memories together."
      "What are your plans for the upcoming [holiday or special occasion]?"
      
      7. Paying the Bill:
      
      "Should we split the bill evenly, or does anyone want to pay separately?"
      "I'll take care of the tip. Does anyone have cash?"
      "Let me get this one. You can treat next time."
      "Are we ready for the bill, or would anyone like dessert or another drink?"
      "Thanks for joining me for dinner, everyone. It's my treat this time."

  Remember, amazing writers! Don't be too descriptive as the readers might get distracted from the plot/story and some might have to reread the paragraph over and over again because the words are too deep/hard to understand.
  
  It is important to first determine the themw of what you're writing. Is the story light? Choose words that feel free and light.
  Example: A light story
  
  The breeze meandered against her porcelein skin, sending cold yet sweet chills down to her spine. Her golden hair danced gracefully as she yelled, "I'm the king of the world!" with her arms up high and her ocean eyes gleaming. 
  
  Even if words are well, just words, they still have the power to activate the reader's five senses; smell, touch, sight, hearing, taste.

  but if a character is suddenly realising that theyre in love with their best friend and cant help but admire how their hair flows in the wind and the slight sparkle in their eye that only comes out when the weathers nice, then a long detailed moment makes sense because the character is noticing all these things themselves and has the time to linger mentally on those details

The reason I put that much detail was because it was early in the story, and I wanted to set the expectations of the reader to understand the hard magic system using real world physics concepts to understand the function of the magic embedded in the arrow. I also wanted to introduce the badass mentor character and how overwhelmingly power she is so the reader would see the highest tier of what mortals can achieve, and expect the protagonist to be at least this powerful by the end of the story.

  How do you study vocabulary in a your target language?

    ↳ **@K3rr1g4nEXE** (👍4 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NQZYL39JEFo&lc=Ugw7Apb0rvBYdhvDVYB4AaABAg.9cchAGsb5QY9frTHxf7VSc
      right now i just look for lists of words on the internet in target language. maybe ill practice words for animals one minute and then common words the next. sometimes ill practice words that start with certain letters. sometimes ill practice words that are relevant to me and not just words that are common in the the language - words common to me I'd say.     ↳ **@sylwiawajda9866** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NQZYL39JEFo&lc=Ugw7Apb0rvBYdhvDVYB4AaABAg.9cchAGsb5QY9jeTeUS5EXg
      In my opinion, there is no better way to memorize new vocabulary than getting to know them thanks to somebody else in a daily conversation. Especially if you're excited or there's a story or some situation attached. Once you learnt a word this way, you are likely to remember it forever. Sometimes I even remember how and when I've learnt some particular word😅
    ↳ **@capuchinosofia4771** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NQZYL39JEFo&lc=Ugw7Apb0rvBYdhvDVYB4AaABAg.9cchAGsb5QY9rvkkgDRBPI
      I search for new words and try to add them to the vocab I already know by making many sentences or questions with them to ingrain them in my brain.

      So I'm a medical student in India.
      
      Here there is a "tradition" where seniors give juniors punishments (situps, pushups, beatings you know normal stuff lol) if they are unable to recognize a senior's name from the photo they show. And, as juniors we are not supposed to make eye contact with the seniors if we see them in person. Actually, we're never supposed to meet them either unless we're called by them to do their jobs.
      
      So as juniors, we had to sit down and memorize the seniors' names and faces from Facebook and Instagram so as to not get thoroughly grilled. And well the undergraduate course in India is for 5 years, so you can imagine the amount of names we had to memorize as juniors. I had memorized everything but then they started showing their childhood photos, which we could do nothing for. I had to become a "murga" (basically squat and put your arms behind your legs bring them up through your knees and grab your ears) many times.
      
      I'm in third year now so it's much better for me now haha.
      
      Tldr: I had to sit down with a chart and memorize names and faces of people I had never met/barely seen the faces of.

      Both recall and exposure are important. Can you try to do exposure only? Sure, but it is less efficient, since recall has been shown to be the single most important factor for acquiring and retaining vocabulary. If you really hate doing a few minutes of recall every day to balance things out, then by all means don't do it. But please don't try to convince others that it's more efficient because science does not support that claim.

  My approach is to write down all the expressions I want to learn in a journal.  I group expressions with the same purpose of use under the same category. For instance, if the purpose of use of the expressions is giving advice (category), these expressions will be together: your best bet, you'd be better off, you may want to, it's in your best interest, and so on and so forth with all the expressions. This gives me a sense of direction and organization. When I hear one of the expressions under a category, I remember all the expressions that belong to that specific category. The bottom line is you have to prioritize to remember (sense) the category (purpose of use) over the expressions so that during a conversation, you're not trying to remember a specific expression ...once you need to say something with a specific purpose, the expressions will come to mind.

**@norabalogh5910** (👍33 · 2022-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NQZYL39JEFo&lc=UgyXOougI8LBBjFC3r14AaABAg
  This is interesting and it's one possibility. 
  
  But personally I do like spend a VERY LIMITED AMOUNT OF TIME doing conscious vocabulary review, throughout my language-learning process until I am quite advanced (i.e. until I get to the C1 level or so).  I have a natural feeling that some conscious review of some important words is helpful in getting them to "stick" eventually. And as long as vocabulary practice remains a minor activity, it's actually reasonably interesting and enjoyable!  (By the way, it isn't my expectation that, having reviewed a certain word for a while I will now know it forevermore and even be able to actively use it.  Review is just another way of "playing" with words and expressions and getting more exposure to them...).
  
  
  Here's how I do my vocabulary review for Hungarian (my fifth language, currently at the B1 level).  First of all, I'm using lingq, and since new vocabulary is stored there anyway, and Lingq has a reasonable and simple SRS associated with it, I use it as my review tool. My target is to make sure that the time I spend at vocabulary review is limited to something like 10-15 minutes a day out of, in my case, 1-2 hours a day of language study/exposure.  
  
  So how do I use an SRS effectively while limiting the time spent?  Simple: I only review a very small subset of the words I lingq!  Every day I will flag a maximum of 1-5 words with a tag I've called "review".  I always filter on this tag when doing reviews and only review words that are due AND that have the "review" tag attached. I also add information to the "Note" field of these lingqs at the time I attach the "review" tag: I look up the word in the dictionary and include the standard, "dictionary" form of this word or expression as well as the full paragraph of surrounding text and I look at these later when I do my review.   Also, I'll add that I only use the "flashcard" option for reviewing, that is, I try to remember what the word means using only with the tiny snippet of context Lingq shows you.
  
  If it takes me more than 12-15 minutes to review all "due" vocabulary, then I stop adding new words with the "review" tag for a little while.  I also regularly remove the review tag from older vocabulary that I know quite well (for now), aiming to keep to a maximum of no more than 300-400 words with the "review" tag attached.
  
  How do I decide what vocabulary to tag for review?  I go by gut feel and pick words that seem useful to me.  I usually tag vocabulary associated with a particular source, picking only texts that are right at my level, because they are more likely to contain the right vocabulary for me at this stage of the game...
  
  Some thoughts anyway.  Different strokes for different folks as they say!!!

      Summary:
      - put minimal effort into studying vocabulary 
      - learn vocab. through reading (LingQ)
      - small portions of spaced repetition of 300-400 unknown and useful words (use tags to keep track of them)
      - review daily (max. 12-15min), delete old vocab. after a while

  I agree to an extent. I’m an American living in Poland and learning Polish. I‘ve been here for about a year with my husband and am on the border of A2/B1. Considering this is the 3rd most difficult language for English speakers to learn I’m quite proud of the fact that I can understand about half of what I hear and can respond to native Polish speakers in simple sentences. 
  
  What I’ve been doing for the last year is keeping a list of very functional words I don’t know in my phone. Every time I don’t know a word, I open up the notes feature in my phone, add the word to my list, and then intentionally memorize it.
  
  Polish is not very intuitive for Native English speakers. Not many words are similar to English and I can hear a word 20 times in a polish conversation and never remember it. But, if I write it down and intentionally memorize it it stays with me forever. It’s been working so far since these words are incredibly functional in everyday conversation. For instance, I’m pregnant right now and have been memorizing so much baby terminology since I’m very motivated. This gets reinforced daily by my environment (for instance, seeing the word on an item in the maternity store) since right now baby-related words are functional. 
  
  Lately I’ve also tried memorizing predetermined lists of words from a small Polish-to-English visual dictionary. This week I’m focusing on the category “wygląd” (appearance) which has many technical terms pertaining to clothing and accessories such as: cotton pads, a dress seam, a necklace chain, nail clippers, dyed hair etc.
  
  These are all functional terms I absolutely should know if I plan on living in Poland long-term, but getting through this list systematically has been proving far more challenging for me. Isn’t it better to memorize all of these lists at once? If not, it may end up taking me years to master Polish! Just some food for thought.

      @Nerian For me learning a language is not a race. The amount of words can be adjusted by the individual. I find a 100 words a month for me to be fairly comfortable to acquire yet not overwhelming where it's going to demotivate me or start to feel like homework.       Yeah I would agree that Kanji is a bit of a tricky one. 
      I previously used Wanikani that sorta just throws radicals, Kanji and vocab at you (in an order where you cover most commonly used ones first, and much more complicated nuances words later), but I found this never seemed to stick for me.
      I instead started studying Kanji using Remember The Kanji which teaches them in an order of common radicals, this way you can see several similar Kanji at once and be able to pick apart the radicals they are constructed of.     ↳ **@Thelinguist [channel author]** (👍2 · 2022-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NQZYL39JEFo&lc=UgwNN3p6WtF9PH07jVd4AaABAg.9cduLmXKq2T9cfhyuajneH

    ↳ **@ta4music459** (👍0 · 2022-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NQZYL39JEFo&lc=UgwNN3p6WtF9PH07jVd4AaABAg.9cduLmXKq2T9cgYPCUxMvB
      I wouldn't worry about it. Except for a very low minority, anyone learning a language as an adult will make "mistakes" forever. But it doesn't matter. My wife speaks my language with what's technically "mistakes" here and there, but I and friends don't really notice - to us she's speaking perfectly. That's because she's communicating perfectly, and in the end that's the only thing that matters. So it feels to us that she's fully proficient. There are also genuine errors which can hold up communication *occasionally*, but that's rare and often quickly sorted out - nothing to worry about.  Sometimes she's putting things in a way "natives" wouldn't - and sometimes that's as good as, or better than the "traditional" way.  I want her to keep those..
      
      And then there's the fact that natives make mistakes all the time too - no wonder, we talk while still making up what we're about to say, there's no way the sentence can come out grammatically "correct". That's part of language. I.e. even grammatically incorrect language isn't really a mistake if it can still get the meaning across (otherwise natives should feel embarrassed all the time. And we never do).
      
      Try to not be mindful about it. Some people find that they speak easier and better after a beer or two, or in a situation where you can't be mindful about it - as that nurse who suddenly had to step into a life-saving situation and her English problems went away - that's from a comment I read the other day). It's because you stop minding.

      ​ @rayflaherty3441  Recall has NOT been shown to be the most important factor actually. When you say science supports this, what science - which research journal and paper are you talking about? Scientific research on language learning is extremely difficult to do and that is why it has a long way to go. The best we have right now are theories that might be true and that's it. The truth is, learning a language is unlike learning anything else and so it's challenging to make scientific conclusions, because there are way too many individual factors. I researched the topic extensively when I was working on my paper on the neuroscience of multilingualism and trust me - the scientific community "kind of knows" some things about language learning, but that's it - no hard cold proof about anything. 
      
      That being said, each polyglot has their own method. In my case and that of Steve (I have been following him for years, so I'm pretty familiar with his method), we do recall through exposure (because getting more input means you see the same words again - which is recall). And many, many others have found that this type of recall is much more efficient for language learning than the usual repetitive, dull methods. 
      
      Language learning isn't like memorizing facts for some exam. Doesn't work that way.

  My comment here is genuinly the BEST and quickest way i learned languages at conversational level is the simplest yet no one ever does it- basically just made 100s of flash cards for the main most common words (adjectives, adverbs, nouns etc) and went through them 10 minutes every day for a few months. By that time i was farmiliar with the most common words to get meaning out of a fair bit of sentences i heard. I then began to watch sitcoms, radio shows etc of that language every day on top of the flashcards and within a year i could understand the language enough to talk/listen to most people in it. All you need to know is the simple main words to get most meanings out of sentences. Even word order doesnt even matter at conversational level most will be able to understand if you just say the main words. People waste too much time learning the language to perfection/correct way too quickly and it overloads their mind.

      ​ @BrianWilesOfficial  If I tried to learn more than one foreign language, I'd worry about mixing up vocabulary. For example, I took Spanish in school, & I'm studying Esperanto now. Because I'm so much more comfortable with Esperanto, if I try to think of how to translate something to Spanish, I always think of at least 1 or 2 words from Esperanto. It doesn't help that there are some words that are the same or very similar, like "esti" (to be). The present tense is "estas", so it's just like "you are" in Spanish. Esperanto also doesn't have the verb conjugation, depending on who you're talking to/about, as Spanish. It only conjugates for tense, so that's another thing I have to try to remember. For the most part, They're very different languages. Esperanto is a little like Romanian: It sounds like a mix of Italian & Russian with some other vocabulary thrown in.

      @xesterbruh  I took 4 years of French and 3 years of Spanish in school. French is harder than Spanish, but still very similar. 
      
      I am now studying Persian, Japanese, Mandarin, and Russian.
      
      The game completely changes when you are studying a language with a different alphabet and writing system. It is significantly harder. 
      
      If you speak ZERO Spanish, you could pick up a book in Spanish and read/pronounce most of what is in the book, even if you don’t know what it means. 80-90%
      
      In French you could do the same thing, but maybe get 60-70% of it because there is some funky pronunciation. 
      
      But pick up a book in Arabic, Farsi, Chinese, or Japanese… you are completely lost. There is no way to have any clue what you’re looking at.
      
      Russian is perhaps more deceiving because many letter look the same, but have a completely different pronunciation. You might think you can read some of it, but you’re going to be 80-90% wrong.

**@intissar_raghd** (👍258 · 2022-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r7VKVXbaj_Y&lc=UgzmmrOnD4PZuq4MeXh4AaABAg
  A little help here guys 🙂👇
  1/ bring up : to start discussing something. Ex: let's bring this up at our next meeting.
  2/ to get across: when you want to help someone understand something or manage to communicate an idea clearly. Ex: he is not good at getting his ideas across.
  3/ jump in : to interrupt , to join a conversation . Ex: jump in if you have any questions.
  3/ butt in: to interrupt a conversation or discussion or someone who is talking. Ex: I was speaking with sue after she lost her job, then jim butts in and start talking about his new promotion.
  4/ blurt out : to say something you're not supposed to say. it's secret. Ex: I'm sorry I just blurt it out! 
  5/ get through to:  to try to call someone and they don't answer. Ex: I'm trying to get through but there's no answer.
  2 meaning: when you are trying to make someone understand what you are trying to say. Ex: it's difficult to get the message through my team because we all work remotely.
  5/ to talk over: to discuss a problem or a plan , usually when you're trying to find a solution , it's when you're a little stuck , you've got talk about some more so that you can come to a resolution or to make it clear. Ex: I know you're upset, let's talk it over tonight when you get home.
  2 meaning: to speak when someone else is speaking, to intentionally interrupt them. Ex: I don't mean to talk over you, but we have already decided what to do.
  6/ talk around: to convince or persuade someone to agree. Ex: I didn't want to go but he succeeded in talking me around.
  7/shut down: to stop someone in the middle of the sentence. Ex: it was kinda awkward, she just shut him down mid-sentence.
  2 meaning, to close something. Usually  permanently, forever. Ex: the restaurant got shut down last year.
  8/ back ( someone) up : to give support by telling other people you're agree with something they said or did. Ex: thanks for backing me up during the meeting.
  9/ look back on (something): to think about the past. Ex: I tried to look back on the mistakes i made in the past and learn from them.
  10/look after (someone): to take care of someone. Ex: who's going to look after your dog when you're away?
  11/ look down on ( someone) : to think you're better of someone or treat someone or something as unimportant or not respect worthy. Ex: it's really common for people who value university education to look down on those who don't have degrees.
  12/ look for ( something): to try to find something. Ex: I'm looking for my keys.
  13/ look forward to (sth): to wait for something and feel excited about it. Ex: I'm looking forward to summer.
  14/ look around or round: to visit a place and see what is there or to explore a place. Ex: before i book the venue I'd like to look around, is that okay? 🙈
  15/ look out : to be careful. Ex: look out! you're about to knock that glass off the bench.
  16/ look out for (so.): to take care of someone. Ex: my nephews are always looking out for each other at school .
  17/ look ( something) up: 1 meaning: search for and find a piece of information in a book or a dictionary. Ex: if you don't know a word look it up in the dictionary.
  2 meaning:  .
  (of a situation) improve. Ex:
  "things seemed to be looking up at last"
  18/ look up to someone: to respect someone and you wanna be like them. Ex: I really look up to my boss.
  19/ look into ( sth.): to investigate something. Ex: the police looked into his business dealing.
  20/  look over ( sth.): To examine something usually quickly. Ex: I'll look over the report and let you know if you want to add anything.
  21/ look through (sth.) :  to read or briefly examine some of the pages of (a book, magazine, etc.) Ex: She was looking through a magazine as she waited in the doctor's office. 2 meaning : to look at the different parts of (a collection or group of things) I looked through all his letters. 
  22/ come down with: to catch a cold or illness... Ex: they came with Cold.
  23/ fight off: to defend oneself against (someone or something) by fighting or struggling : to avoid being harmed or overcome by (someone or something) Ex: she came down with a cold but  she was able to fight it off quickly.
  24/ pass away: to die. Ex: my mother passed away give years ago.
  25/ dip into : to spend some of your money usually it's money that you're saving for specific purpose. Ex:  I'll have to dip into my savings 🙁
  26/get by : manage with difficulty to live or accomplish something. Ex: even though Tim has been without work for six months they have been getting by .
  27/ go without: manage without something one usually has. to live or continue without having (something) Ex: how long can a human being go without sleep?
  28/to mentioned or talked about in conversation. Ex: if anything important come up. I'll tell you about it later. 2 meaning: to approach or go towards someone especially if they are on high level than you are . Ex: come up on stage and collect your award. 3 meaning: if something comes up, it becomes available. Ex: a new opportunity has come up and we need to take it. 4 meaning: if a problem or an issue come up , it happens and we need to deal with immediately. Ex: something has just come up so I need to cancel my appointment .
  29/ come in : to enter a room or building. Ex: the tv was so loud he didn't notice me come in. 2 meaning: to arrive. Ex: the train come in at Three o'clock. 3 meaning:  it can also be used when talking about clothing or fashion. Ex: these shirts come in three colors.
  30/ come out : something that was previously unknown and becomes known. Ex: after 10 years the truth finally came out. 2 meaning: to appear. Ex: there was a dead tree coming out of the water.3 meaning: the release of a product. Ex: the New album will come out in Jun. 4 meaning: to go somewhere with someone for a social event. Ex: do you wanna come out with us Friday night.
  31/ come on : to hurry up. Ex: come on, we're gonna be late. 2 meaning: to encourage someone. Ex: come on, you can do it . 3 meaning: it's used when you don't believe what someone said. Ex: come on, that's not true! 4 meaning: to start working. Ex: the light in the bathroom just came on. 5 meaning: it's also used when you're referring to a sickness that is just starting to develop. Ex: I think I got a cold coming on.
  32/come down: when something moves in a downward direction ⬇️. Ex:  there was a big storm last night and many of the trees came down . 2 meaning: it's used when you're talking to someone who is higher than you , perhaps in a tree 🌴. Ex: come down here ! 3 meaning : it's used when something reduces , often the price. Ex: We're coming down everything in-store for the next seven days, so come on by for the best deals in town!
  33/ come down on ( someone): to punish someone become they didn't perform as expected. Ex: my Boss came down on me really hard because I didn't finish the report in time.
  34/ come over: to describe a movement from a place to another. Ex: why don't you come over My house for dinner?
  35/ come back: used when somebody or something returns to a place or an original state. Ex: I'll come back a half and na hour to get you . Ex2: I thought I got rif of my cold bit I think it's coming back.
  36/ brush up on : to update or improve skills. Ex: I got the job at the polishing company! But I really need to brush up on my editing skills. 
  37/ to turn down: to say no to something or refuse. Ex: they offered me a tickes to the conference. But I had to turn them down because it's my son's birthday 🎉
  38/cheer up : to improve your mood. Ex: he was very sad so i told him a joke to cheer him up 😊
  39/back up : to provide extra support. Ex: she backed up her stories with photographic evidence.
  40/ dress up : to wear a fancy dress for specific party or weeding.... Ex: I've got to dress up because I'm going on a date .
  41/cook up : to prepare (food) for eating especially quickly. Ex: I can cook up some hamburgers. 2 meaning: to get an idea ready, to do something maybe a surprise party 🤷. Ex: I'm cooking up a plan . interesting. 
  45/ whip up : to excite (someone or something) : to cause (someone or something) to feel strong emotions about something. Ex: His speech whipped up the crowd. 2 informal : to cause or create (something). Ex:  She was trying to whip up some enthusiasm. 3 informal : to produce or prepare (a meal) very quickly. Ex:I can whip a meal up in no time.
  46/ dream up : to think of a new idea or to imagine someone new. Ex: I dreamt up an entire neaw plan for the party.
  47/Set up : to plan or organise something. Ex: I set up my studio every time I need to film a lesson.
  48/ make up : to invent a lie 🤥 or a story. Ex: don't believe her , she always makes up a stories. 2 meaning: to repair your relationship. Ex: Sarah and John had an other argument but they always make up.
  49/ come up with: to suggest or think of an idea or solution. Ex: Several of the members have come up with suggestions of their own. 
  50/heal up : when a surgery get better. Ex: his broken leg healed up really quickly.
  51/ sober up : to become less drunk or intoxicated. Ex: coffee and breakfast will help you to sober up.
  Patch up: to fix something whole again. Ex: I'm going to patch up my the hole in my jumper. So I can wear it 😉
  52/ finish up : to complete. Ex: finish up your food.
  53/ wrap up : complete, to finish up . Ex: it's almost time to wrap up this lesson .
  54/Drink up : finish your drink quickly
  56/Eat up : finish your food quickly.

  8. *Logical*

  9. *Traditional*

  10. *Brief*

  11. *Begin*

  12. *Solution*

      - Way out  
  
  13. *Show*

      - Showcase  
  
  14. *Strong*

  - Nowadays (~Introduction)(At the beginning of a sentence)
  - I would argue that (~in my opinion)
  - In spite of (~Although) (in spite of + noun //in spite of + gerund (- ing verb)// in spite of + the fact that ....)
  - For instance (~for example)
  - Due to (~because)
  - by contrast (~However) (link 2 sentences together)
  - As a result of (~therefore) (At the beginning of a sentence or in the middle)
  - Ensure (~make sure)
  - Enable (Be able)
  - Hence (~therefore) (in the middle)
  - lack (~not enough)
  - invaluable (~very valuable)
  - paramount (~Very important) (It is of paramount...)
  - significant (~large)
  - if (conditional/complex sentence)
  
  Happy study...👍

  Part 1 (Simple Personal Questions — About You)
  	•	“I live in [city]…”
  	•	“I work as [job]…”
  	•	“I study at [university]…”
  	•	“I’d say I generally prefer…” (for simple preference questions)
  	•	“I’d rather…” (alternative way to express preference)
  
  ⸻
  
  Part 2 (Cue Card — Long Talk about Past Experiences or Examples)
  	•	“Well, I remember…”
  	•	“Back in [year]…”
  	•	“It happened when…”
  	•	“Certainly, for example, last year I…”
  	•	“Sure, for example…”
  	•	“Actually, for example…”
  
  ⸻
  
  Part 3 (Discussion — Opinions, Hypothetical, and Complex Answers)
  	•	“Actually, in my opinion, it depends on…”
  	•	“Well, I think…”
  	•	“I would probably choose…” (for hypothetical questions)
  	•	“If I could…, I would…”
  	•	“Well, it depends on the person because…”
  	•	“It depends on the situation…”
  	•	“That’s an interesting question. I think…”
  	•	“That’s a tough one. I guess…”
  	•	“I’m not entirely sure, but if I had to guess…”
  	•	“That’s a tricky one. It might depend on…”

  Preference: Direct statement’ I generally prefer / I would rather’
  Opinion: Conversational ‘Actually I think In my opinion’
  Past experience : Start with recall / story mode ‘ Well I remember last year I visited’
  Hypothetical:  Indicate imaginary scenario ‘ I would probably choose’
  Comparative: ‘ In depends on the ‘
  Basic question/ chitchat type : Direct answer
  Deeper part 3 questions: ‘ That’s an interesting question’
  Personal example: ‘ Certainly, for example’ 
  Unpredictable:  ‘ I’m not entirely sure ‘

  Summary : "Be a British person in speaking- yeah, its a metaphor." 
  #ThreeRules : - 
  1) In Work or learning or career questions give directly what you do and what plans you have...bcoz merit is apex thing- that's supreme bcoz "individuality is the modern forte and it demands independent decision making" 
  2) For society, experiences, opinions - Avoid direct answers bcoz if you are direct..it is highly likely a person has a tendency of being an anarchist, narcissistic or conservative or simply put a toxic/ignorant person. So represent consciousness about wide range of opinions, values, feelings and experiences that people can have- bcoz as a global citizen opting for IELTS you cannot afford to remain in your own bubble or even give the impression as it might affect you/ your community/ your country's image & Anti- immigration narrative might build against you.
  3) Unpredictable question : Is there God?/ Is Ai harmful?/ Is vegan thing actually sustainable for ecosystem? 
  - Just start upon the unknown with..... "I am not quite sure to what extent..... But (in my opinion) or (But as we know)... etc "

**@md.rakibulislam8064** (👍7 · 2025-09-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WP2LcgMq-_8&lc=UgwZbeksyGf4Xe7SaFt4AaABAg
  1. Preferences
  🔹 Formula: Answer + Explanation
   Q: Do you prefer to study in the morning or at night?
   A: I would say I generally prefer mornings, simply because my mind feels fresher and I can focus better without distractions.
  
  2. Opinion
  🔹 Formula: Filler (well, actually) + Statement of opinion
   Q: Do you think children should learn to cook at school?
   A: Actually, in my opinion, it depends on the school system. Cooking is a valuable life skill, but it might take time away from academic subjects.
  
  3. Past Experience
  🔹 Formula: Direct recall + Answer
   Q: Describe a time when you travelled somewhere new.
   A: Well, I remember last year I visited Cox’s Bazar for the first time, and it was amazing to see the longest sea beach in the world.
  
  4. Hypothetical
  🔹 Formula: Would + Verb
   Q: If you could live in any city, where would you choose?
   A: I would probably choose London, because it’s vibrant and offers plenty of career opportunities.
  
  5. Multiple Sides / Unsure
  🔹 Formula: It depends + SIDE A + SIDE B + Personal angle
   Q: Do you think people are happier in cities or rural areas?
   A: Well, it depends on the person. Some people enjoy the convenience of cities, while others prefer the peace of rural life. If I were choosing, I’d probably go with a quieter place.
  
  6. Deeper Part 3 Question
  🔹 Formula: Bridging phrase + Opinion/Explanation
   Q: Why do some people choose to live in cities rather than rural areas?
   A: That’s an interesting question. I think many people choose cities for better jobs and education, while rural areas attract those who value nature and community life.
  
  7. Personal Example
  🔹 Formula: Bridging word + Example
   Q: Can you give an example of when you learned something new?
   A: Certainly. For example, last year I started learning Photoshop, and it helped me a lot with my business presentations.
  
  8. Unpredictable / Broad Question
  🔹 Formula: I’m not entirely sure, but if I had to guess…

  Excellent rundown. Professional (nonfiction) editor myself and I'm still guilty of some of these.
  A tip I've given some of the writers I work with (especially ESL): If you're worried a sentence is getting into run-on territory, read it out loud under your breath at a normal pace. If you find yourself wheezing by the end, split the sentence roughly where you started running out of breath. Punctuation is meant to replicate on paper the pauses we naturally take when speaking. 
  
  Also, could I possibly request a video about how to jot down the first page or two of a novel? Not just the opening plot beat, but literally the first few hundred words. Do you have any advice as to how to get past those first few paragraphs/how to make them count?
    ↳ **@foxonfire7** (👍12 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N70D6xP0aQo&lc=UgwRrG7eIF1SS6oZqrV4AaABAg.9k0aQZuiIOt9pTIwa9hjpC
      I am a begginer so take this with a gracious grain of salt but i can give you a technice that worked for me with writing chapters and filling that dreaded blank page. 
      
      Set a timer for 5-15 minutes and write without a paus untill it rings. Dont pay attention to finding the right word repetition or using cliche similies or anything like that, just write. I find that once you have something in front of you it becomes much easier to write.   Guilty of all 12.
  
  It took me over 10 years to break most of these habits, but old habits die hard.
  
  What I've found useful is whenever I use a starting action, like in the example you shared: "Elizabeth started to laugh." I find a starting action helps when you want to have it interrupted by a character.
  
  "Elizabeth started to laugh... until John gave her a death stare. Then it wasn't funny."
  
  I also wholeheartedly agree on cutting unnecessary words. In one sentence it's not a big deal and is easily forgivable. In a 90,000 page novel the work feels bloated for no reason. If a word is going to be included, it should be a detail with a specific purpose.
  
  When I had to write a tribute to someone who had passed, I used a sentence: "And taught her daughter how to calculate sales prices at Dunham's."
  
  I could have just said and "calculate sales prices." The sentence can survive on its own.
  
  But I added Dunham's so the people local to the area might remember the time period when that store existed. I would have left Dunham's out if it had been a generic chain like Wal Mart. But because this particular Dunham's was a specific store during a specific time period, I added the detail for those who remembered the store.
  
  Since I manage a website, I also found using a plugin called Yoast SEO helped improve my writing significantly because it has tools to identify passive voice and wordy sentences.   Passive voice can be really useful for creating tension, subtext or being efficient with words, particularly when it leaves out the person doing the action altogether. This can be because we don't know who did something: 'The jewels were stolen sometime before dawn.'
  
  Or don't want to say (eg avoiding blame): 'Dad, your favourite mug got broken!' 
  
  Or we're building suspense: 'The door had been left ajar. Voices were hushed as she called out, "Hello?". 
  
  Or it's just not necessary to say who did it: 'The house was painted a flat, dismal grey that matched the rain-filled sky.'
  
  It's a really powerful tool that we often don't notice we're using, so not always bad or a 'no'. 🙂
    ↳ **@thethmooteresa** (👍2 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N70D6xP0aQo&lc=Ugwwv2nXzWCfUtGEeQ14AaABAg.9og2Fijn2qE9wPqgpGd1tg
      Absolutely 🎉❤ know the rules, to  break them when you want to 😊
    ↳ **@Synist3Twist** (👍2 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N70D6xP0aQo&lc=Ugwwv2nXzWCfUtGEeQ14AaABAg.9og2Fijn2qEAD34SocBqau
      'The house was painted a flat, dismal grey that matched the rain-filled sky.'
      This actually is not the passive voice. It's not considered passive voice when you are describing the quality of an object. Think about it, the subject is doing the adjective perfectly actively, it's just that the verb is a state of being and therefore cannot be stated otherwise. "painted a flat, dismal grey" is actually an adjective, the house wasn't painting in the past, the house simply IS (past tense) painted.
      
      'The house is/was blue.' You can't active voice this. And it's not passive voice either. It's simply a description. This is a big problem with the passive/active voice argument: trying to bend over backwards to make every sentence active voice is literally impossible and adds nothing. You can fancy this up often. 
      'The house emanated the color of the sky, filling one's vision like looking up on a clear summer's day'
      
      But you don't always want to do this. It's obnoxious went a writer can't just tell you things sometimes. So there is balance in this particular usage.
      
      Overall, you just have to try not to use passive voice unnecessarily when a better option is available. I think the most common is the use of the word "had". If you're using had, you had better be sure you can't possibly use anything else, and you should probably avoid stringing them together unless you're building to a present event.

  Thought this might help others too.
  1) length
  2) word size/obscurity 
  3) tone of words
  4) passive, filtered, simile
  5) body parts
  6) "was x-ing"
  7) "started" & other unnecessary words.
  
  Examples of filter type words:
  Thought
  Knew
  Saw
  Felt
  Wondered
  Smelled
  Tasted

  21:30 I'd like to add something about Vocabulary that I learned on test readings.
  Using a term correctly can lead to confusion if the reader doesn't have the same understanding of that word.
  It's interesting that now it's trivial to look up unfamiliar words immediately, before going on with the next sentence.  When I first read the original Sherlock Holmes stories, I wrote down words to look up later.  Now, reading on a tablet or e-paper reader, I can point to a word and get a definition (or translation) instantly.  This should remove the barrier toward using a higher vocabulary or highly specific terminology, pushing some readers to learn, and not talking down to those already more familiar with the subject.

  FYI: As far as sensory info, a pro tip is to use that to cover more than one goal. Of course, everything we write should serve at least one of the following three purposes: world building; development of character; or move the plot along.
  Since we are bombarded by sensory information all the time (probably millions of them a second) the ones we choose to write about should have some meaning for the character.
  
  For example: the tang of damp earth, etc. could become
  
  The tang of damp earth and the ferment of damp earth evoked memories of .....
  
  In this case, our writing serves two purposes: world building and character development.
  
  Thankis, I hope this is helpful

**@jamesaritchie1** (👍6 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N70D6xP0aQo&lc=UgxMZfEc2DscKI2gQ2h4AaABAg
  I spent thirty years earning a living as a creative writer, though most of what I wrote was behind the scenes ghosting for a publisher, or using a double pseudonym.  But I sold five novels under my own name, and close to a hundred short stories.  Funny, but selling short stories to paying magazines is harder than selling a novel.  I had to stop about twenty years ago because it's tough to write when you're in a coma, and have a wrecked body.  I came out of the coma, but it took so long to make my body work again, and to be able to sit down and think through the pain that I decided it was time to stop.
  
  But I do know your advice is excellent.  I would note that while such programs as Hemingway can be helpful, they will not produce good, publishable writing.  A writer should never blindly follow any program I've tested.  Or blindly follow and grammar check program.    Perfect grammar and perfect punctuation does not mean good writing. 
  
  Story comes first.  A good story is essential.  But character, dialogue, and description are the things that make a story good.  Plot and story are not the same thing, but too many new writers don't understand this.   Many, many top writers never plot, never outline, yet they tell a great story.
  
  I also worked as an editor now and then, most often helping an editor friend whittle a slush pile down to size.  Another thing new writers probably don't know is that not all agents are created equal, and editors do not automatically treat what they receive from different agents the same way.  Some agent seldom send anything that isn't very good, even if it isn't quite right for a given publisher.  These agents build a reputation for quality, and editors trust the,
  
  Other agents, well, not so much.  Thier submission are treated like slush because while they occasionally have something worthwhile, you can bet that at least nine out of ten will be very low quality.  
  
  Anyway, one very big mistake new writers make, at least those who want to go through guarded gates of large, traditional publishers, is thinking they have to set the story in some exotic city they've never been to, and don't know how to research.   
  
  I sold a story to Ellery Queen's Mystery Magazine called "Wild Strawberries."    The POV character is a seventeen-year-old who lives in a tiny farm town of about one hundred people.  To cut this short, he murders his pregnant girlfriend, blames it on his best friend, who actually believes he's responsible, and then lives happily ever after.  It's told in first person.  The editor said she would normally have rejected such a story, but the description was so good that she couldn't pass it up.  She even mentions the description in the introductory blurb that introduced the story.  The description was so right because I actually grew up in that tiny town.
  
  No exotic location I'd never visited, just a town in the middle of nowhere that I knew perfectly.
  
  There's a saying that covers novels and short stories.  "Editors want something just like everything else. . .only different."   It's true.  There's god different, and there's bad different.  Good different sells.
  
  Another story I sold to Ellery Queen was called "The Real West."   It's more or less a typical story except for one thing; The POV character is me.  I used myself as the protagonist in a crime story.  Not many writers do that.  I can't remember seeing it, though I'm sure it's been done.  I believe using myself as the POV character made that particular story ring true.  In fact, most of it was true.  The ending was fiction, but everything else actually happened.  I did this once more in Ellery Queen, and it worked well enough that I sold stories to a few other magazines using this same technique.
  
  I guess what I'm saying is that for a new writer, what and where and who we know counts for a lot.  
  
  Really do love your advice.  Selling fiction takes more than good sentences, of course, but that's always a good place to start.

**@tomlewis4748** (👍11 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N70D6xP0aQo&lc=Ugx-qVRUwc-Anf9RdJt4AaABAg
  The filtering advice makes sense for 3rd-p stories and those that are more plot-driven. The desire is to move the focus slightly more toward the events and slightly more away from the character's experience and the authorial narrator commentary.
  
  I disagree about 'filtering' when it applies to 1st-P and the story is more character-driven. The desire there is to move the focus more toward the character's experience and a bit away from the events themselves.
  
  In both situations, the story still gets prime focus, but if we compare 'I saw the tail of a fox sticking out from the brush' with 'The tail of a fox stuck out from the brush', the difference between those two in 1st-P is not at all the same as the difference between them in 3rd-p, as far as the effect they have on the story and the reader experience.
  
  'Rebecca saw …' is a statement from the author/narrator, who does not play a part in the events at all, so removing a filter word in 3rd-p does make a certain amount of sense, as it can help make the author ego much more invisible, which if not invisible, can distract from the story.
  
  In 1st-P, the story is about the character's experience, and readers are bonded closer to the protagonist than they are to the story, bc in 1st-P everything is delivered to the reader directly through the protagonist/narrator rather than through the author.
  
  So what would be considered 'filter' words there actually help keep the focus where we want it—on the character's experience. 'I saw …' is not an 'authorial intrusion', it is directly shown as an experience the character is having, which is the goal. 'The tail of a fox …' in 1st-P only creates more distance between the reader and the protagonist. And in 1st-P, that is NOT the goal.
  
  The takeaway here is that advice regarding 'filter' words differs in whether it will help your story or actually hurt your story, depending on the POV, the balance between character-driven and plot-driven, and how the story is told. The bottom line is that advice on 'filter' words greatly depends, and simply abhorring them isn't always an automatic improvement. It can actually be a detriment to not use these words for certain ways of writing your story.
  
  Suggestions and guidelines are fine, but there are no 'rules' that can be applied in a one-size-fits-all fashion to your story. Every single case is an individual judgment call, which applies to all artistic decisions. There are no shortcuts.
  
  I feel that this is an important concept for a writer to understand, and to NOT blindly assume that 'filter' words are automatically problematic, bc they ARE not.

  The instruction in this video is for amateur writers engaged in writing genre fiction (melodrama) and nonfiction aimed at the mass market.  In other words, works written for an eighth grade reading level.  If you write for adults with a brain, your thoughts and your sentences will necessarily be more complex and nuanced.  Henry James, Charles Dickens, Marcel Proust and William Faulkner (to name only a few) wrote long, complex sentences with multiple dependent clauses and heightened vocabulary for a public conditioned to read polysyllabic prose.  Their works appear among the most important novels ever written. 
  
  But that was then.   Such authors would have difficulty  being published today.  Publishers are in the business of making money, not art, and they publish books today aimed at the barely literate.  The sad truth is that the contemporary reading public is conditioned by TV, video games, and the ever lower standards of our public school system to read monosyllables that express simple, often infantile ideas.  Therefore, if you are writing for the mass market, the advice in this video is on point.  Conversely, if you are writing for educated people, you write to their level of proficiency.  Know your audience and write accordingly, but with one eye on your editors demographic.

**@Mathew1345-4** (👍4 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N70D6xP0aQo&lc=UgzGBoTecc-8Hoj_AfZ4AaABAg
  Certainly! Here are examples for each of the given writing tips:
  
  1. Avoid confusingly complex sentences:
     Original: The convoluted labyrinth of corridors within the ancient castle, with its myriad of intersecting pathways, posed a significant challenge to the explorers as they attempted to navigate their way to the hidden treasure.
     Simplified: The ancient castle's maze-like corridors made it difficult for the explorers to find the hidden treasure.
  
  2. Set the Tone with word choices:
     Tone: Formal
     Original: The dinner reception shall commence promptly at seven o'clock in the evening.
     Tone: Casual
     Revised: Dinner starts at 7 PM sharp.
  
  3. Avoid passive voice:
     Passive: The cake was eaten by the children.
     Active: The children ate the cake.
  
  4. Remove Filtering:
     Original: I believe that we should consider the possibility of attending the conference.
     Revised: We should consider attending the conference.
  
  5. Set the pace with sentence length:
     Original: The sun was setting behind the mountains, casting long shadows across the valley, painting the sky in hues of orange, pink, and purple, creating a breathtakingly beautiful scene that filled the onlookers with awe.
     Revised: The setting sun painted the sky in brilliant hues, filling the valley with beauty.
  
  6. Avoid body parts taking action:
     Original: His eyes scanned the room for any signs of danger.
     Revised: He scanned the room for any signs of danger.
  
  7. Reduce "was -ing" construction:
     Original: He was running towards the finish line.
     Revised: He ran towards the finish line.
  
  8. Keep the wording natural:
     Original: Utilize instead of use.
     Revised: Use instead of utilize.
  
  9. Cut unnecessary similes:
     Original: Her smile was like a ray of sunshine on a rainy day.
     Revised: Her smile brightened the room.
  
  10. Use vocabulary level strategically:
      Audience: Children
      Original: The accumulation of precipitation created a puddle on the ground.
      Audience: Adults
      Revised: The rain formed a puddle on the ground.
  
  11. Avoid starting actions:
      Original: She started to write a letter to her friend.
      Revised: She wrote a letter to her friend.
  
  12. Cut out unnecessary words:
      Original: In my opinion, I believe that we should consider the possibility of attending the conference.
      Revised: I believe we should consider attending the conference.

**@Magistream** (👍0 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N70D6xP0aQo&lc=UgwKl3T_vY85rFPsMjB4AaABAg
  26:48  First off, I wanted to say a big thank you for this video cause it very much did help me recontextualise a few things and made me think about my shortcomings, strengths, and my own creative voice.
  
  1. Complex Sentences. I think one thing I can struggle with is the use of flowery language or prose. Sometimes I can get a little more long-winded than I need to while describing certain things. So I have to think about what the situation is, and if more descriptive sentences are even the way to go.
  
  3. Passive Voice. I think you're right about Passive Voice and that most of the time writers want to align themselves more on the side of Active Voice to engage the reader. But there is some benefit to giving Antagonistic characters Passive Voice when using Third Person Omniscient, so as to prime the audience for responses during combat. Though, I'd need to reread my passages to see if I might be giving the reader too much unnecessary and unengaging Passive Voice.
  
  4. Filtering. I could see myself using some Filtering when it's not needed, but I am writing Third Person Omniscient so there is a bit of a degree of having to make sure the audience is attached to what's going on when I switch so often, even during single chapters. But it's a skill I need to develop and make sure I'm not expecting too much of the audience and doing my job to make it easy for them.
  
  9. Simile. I think my biggest writing sin as far just literal words-on-the-page writing is after I do action scenes. I think my action scenes are the best part of my work, but the caveat is that I switch from prose when not in action, to frank, hyper-specific details. After a fight scene is over, I often struggle to make my writing interesting again and do too much: 'He did this.' 'She did that.' kinda stuff. My crutch is using Similes when I catch myself being too frank after action scenes. So I need to hold myself more accountable in this regard.
  
  11. Starting Action. This is probably the only thing I mildly disagree with in the video, but again, I agree more than I don't about the subject. The function of a Starting Action is to prep the audience. "She leaped over the banister, left hand wound back, ready to deliver a Hail Mary haymaker right into his teeth." This being said, if you commit to a Starting Action, you have to understand that as the writer, you now have to either deliver, or deliberately subvert the audience expectation that you set up. "Except no she didn't. Her foot caught on the railing and her teeth took the whooping instead as she faceplanted utterly in front of everyone on the sidewalk." You can do a lot with Starting Action, and if you're actually trying to tell action-focused stories, or stories that have a lot of action in them, you should be willing to play with these concepts. But you don't want to spam them for sure. And using Starting Action at all invariably means there's at least two parts to that writing convention, so part two has to be worth it.
  
    Thanks again! This video really did help!

      @Terik17  That's a tricky balance to strike that doesn't get talked about much. More literary works really don't have much of the character's direct POV and the more genre stories are much heavier in it. I find amateurs tend to use character POV narration far too heavily. 
      
      MC direct thoughts are something I used to use way too much and had to minimize. It's not a bad thing, but it doesn't play well for readers in most instances unless the story is really focused in that way.

      ​ @dgage1776  Depends on the story, but I wouldn't say actions lead the way, exactly. Actions, descriptions, and dialog are all used as necessary. I certainly don't stick to any strict rule, but I try to vary it as best I can so it doesn't become repetitive. 
      
      Some parts will be more dialogue heavy, sure, but two characters just speaking at length to one another for 5 full pages can lose a reader's interest (unless that's some super captivating dialogue). Just like bare actions can be dull or overly elaborate descriptions can bog you down. Just needs enough balance to keep things moving and engaging.

      ​ @megbennett107   filter words are extra verbs like thinks/wonders/sees/looks/feels etc that add an extra layer between what the character is experiencing, making it feel less immediate to the reader. ex. "I see him walk outside." without filter words, it's "He walks outside." or  "I hear music playing" turns into "Music fills the room." or instead of "I think that my mom's gonna be mad if I'm late." you can write "My mom's gonna be mad if I'm late." or even better "My mom's gonna kill me if I'm late again." a lot of the time, we don't need to be told that the character is experiencing a sense or a feeling--just write the experience, without the filter of narration. hope that helps!

      @megbennett107  Np! Yes, filtering words are normally verbs for feelings/senses. Like I saw/I thought/I felt etc. Your example is actually an example of passive tense (which is also mentioned in the video). If we used filter words in your example, it would be something like "I felt myself standing on the sidewalk." which is kind of a weird sentence, but hopefully that explains why filter words aren't always necessary? Or, if you google "Nuts and Bolts: Thought Verbs" by Chuck Palahniuk, that's the very article that I first read about filter words in, and it has tons of examples. It was incredibly helpful to me. Happy writing!

      @xChikyx  I cannot speak to that because I am not a native Spanish speaker. I will not presume to know more about that than you do. However, keep in mind that there are some differences between English and Spanish. For example, you have used the verb estar. Not ser. In English, we only have the one verb "to be". Think about why you said "estaba" and not "fue". Estar indicates a temporary state. We don't have anything like that in English. Is that relevant?
      
      More importantly, you have used the imperfect past tense of estar "estaba". You did not use the preterite tense "estuvo". Why? There is a reason, yes? We don't have imperfect past tense in English. In other words, we have no equivalent to "estaba" in English. We only have "estuvo". 
      
      With "estaba" you are giving an example of a verb tense that doesn't exist in English. So maybe that will help you understand why this is different in English.
      
      When we say "she was walking" it is like saying "ella estuvo caminando." 
      
      fue = was
      estuvo = was
      estaba = no hay en Ingles. No existe en Ingles
      
      What I do know and I can speak to is that "she was walking" and "she walked" both happened in the past. Neither is currently continuing.
      
      If you wanted to indicate that the action was continuing at the present time, you would say she is walking or she walks.
      
      Writing fiction is not the same as the way we commonly speak in casual conversation. In fiction written in past tense, it is usually better to say she walked.
      
      For whatever it's worth, I taught ESL for 3 years.

      To me "She walked to the bathroom." = She reached the bathroom by the time the sentence ended. // "She was walking to the bathroom." = She is still walking to the bathroom as the sentence ends.
      Something similar applies to the dialogue tags. Even the position of the tag and the punctutation changes the whole meaning of the sentence:
      She laughed. "Hi." = She laughed, then she said "hi".
      "Hi," she laughed. = She said "hi" laughing.
      "Hi." She laughed. = She said "hi, then she laughed.
      //
      "Hi," she was saying. = the person was speaking the moment
      the action takes place.
      "Hi," she said. = she finished talking. 
      Again, this is just how I, someone who speaks spanish, reads that. 
      p.s. I would translate "Ella estuvo caminando" as "She was walking", but I would translate "She was walking" as "Ella caminaba." "Estuvo" isn't actually really used, at least not around here. It wouls need more context to show the action already ended. "She was walking last saturday."

      @xChikyx  
      Yes, to you, but it doesn't make sense in English. 
      Your example is lacking context. "She was walking to the bathroom" is missing an ending, it implies something is about to happen in between the time it takes to reach the bathroom. 
      "She walked to the bathroom" is complete and doesn't need an ending. for example:
      "She was walking to the bathroom when a book fell from the top shelf." this more correct than your example due to the ending. If the goal is to write that she made it to the bathroom, "she walked" is always more correct. 
                              
      She laughed "Hi."  =   meaning she laughed whilst saying hi... there shouldn't be a full stop after she laughed, it makes it ambiguous and lacks context. Was she laughing already? If so, why was it written this way which is full of ambiguity. instead it should be closer to  "She laughed, before noticing (x). "Hi," she said."  =  She laughed and then said hi.
      
      "Hi," She laughed  =  meaning she laughed whilst saying hi... again, these are the same.
      "Hi." she laughed  =  grammatically incorrect as full stops don't belong there. 
      "Hi," she was saying  =  grammatically incorrect, she cant be half way through saying hi whilst your applying a verb, unless an action is about to interrupt her---but even then, a more grammatically accurate sentence would be "she was about to say hi when..."  or   "She was greeting (x) before..."
      
      What you've done is replace the verb "Said" with laughed thus making that the new verb. 
      If you don't understand, take this for example:
      
      "No thanks," she murmured.   =  she murmured the words, "no thanks" 
      it does not equate to her saying "No thanks" then murmuring something else like you're implying with laughing.
      They roughly equate to:
      "Hi," She said, whilst laughing.  <  "Hi," She said, laughing.  <  "Hi," She laughed.
      "Hi," She said, whilst murmuring.  <   "HI," She said, murmuring. <  "Hi," She murmured. 
      Except all of these are grammatically incorrect (at best, ambiguous) and should be written as---- "Hi," she (verb).
      
      Again:
      "Hi," she said. Is correct.
      "Hi," She was saying. Is just bad English and doesn't make sense grammatically or tense wise.
      
      
      with your Spanish example, you just proved the lack of context makes the whole sentence "was saying/walking" ambiguous and in majority of cases, wrong. The examples by @ComedorDelrico are correct in regards to English.
      
      I'm unsure why you're trying to enforce Spanish interpretations (in regards to tense) onto English in the first place, it would be similar to me trying to disregard gendered application in Spanish nouns because English doesn't have gendered nouns.

For any non-native who does not know how to think in English, must watch this video to see the reason why it’s not happening. Unfortunately, there are two critical mistakes in our education system which leads to this problem; first one is that we are not taught to learn the language as phrases or sentences but word by word. Second, our education and test system does not measure our 4 skills. Therefore, we can not speak or write as real English speakers do because we are educated so far away from “active learning” structure. **@jumbo2315** (👍16 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CqRloBkyqQs&lc=Ugzlx23n1_YsK_sTV954AaABAg
  What is the difference between collocation and phrasal verbs
    ↳ **@Oxfordonlineenglish1 [channel author]** (👍27 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CqRloBkyqQs&lc=Ugzlx23n1_YsK_sTV954AaABAg.8kbnE1cMI0k8kc9W5hYy3N
      Good question! Collocations include many different types of word combination, for example noun-noun combinations, verb-noun combinations, etc. Phrasal verbs have a very specific definition: they're made of a verb plus an adverb, and the whole phrasal verb has a meaning which is not necessarily connected to either part. For example, the meaning of 'turn up' has no literal connection to the meanings of 'turn' and 'up'.
    ↳ **@ЛидияМайстерчук** (👍2 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CqRloBkyqQs&lc=Ugzlx23n1_YsK_sTV954AaABAg.8kbnE1cMI0k8nOxdxmWrT3
      Phrasal verbs  have  prepositions after  them ,  that  change  their  meaning.  For example:  To look  AT;  To look  AFTER;  To look INTO etc.

**@huonglan4032** (👍0 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CqRloBkyqQs&lc=Ugye4yvgJu7JpbjUbvV4AaABAg
  what is the difference between collocations and idoms and phrases?
    ↳ **@Oxfordonlineenglish1 [channel author]** (👍2 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CqRloBkyqQs&lc=Ugye4yvgJu7JpbjUbvV4AaABAg.9P733Hq3pZo9PBRZWH0bo3
      Hi Huong. A collocation is an expression that has two or more words which fit together in a conventional way. An idiom is an expression with two or more words that have a meaning different from the meanings of the individual words. A phrasal verb is a verb + preposition or adverb. Please watch our lessons on these topics for more details: https://www.oxfordonlineenglish.com/phrasal-verbs-for-business, https://www.oxfordonlineenglish.com/phrasal-verbs, https://www.oxfordonlineenglish.com/business-english-phrases-idioms.

      Hi there. Yes, sometimes a proper noun can be added to a collocation to specify more details.   Collocations are like phrasal verbs?
    ↳ **@Oxfordonlineenglish1 [channel author]** (👍0 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CqRloBkyqQs&lc=UgxpxJgjm6v0Ci2Z3V14AaABAg.9DnW19fQtNY9DtZ4SqgN7F
      Hi Julio. They are similar. Collocations are two words that are used together. They 'collocate' which means to put together in a proper order. For example, we wouldn't say 'do a mistake' or 'make my hair'. Phrasal verbs are word pairs with a verb + preposition, verb + adverb, or verb + adverb + preposition. For example: 'grow up', 'put on', and 'put up with'. Hope this helps you!

      Hi Ritu, 'He will have forgotten,' means in the future, this will be done at a certain point.   When I stepped out onto the old wooden dock, a breathtaking sight, more beautiful than any painting, lay before me. The first rays of the rising sun were shyly peeking out from behind the horizon. The ocean was stagnant, an indigo sheet of glass glittering in the morning light. I inhaled deeply and the salty fragrance of the sea filled me. I would never have been able to experience this back in the city, surrounded by the incessant beep beeping of cars and the unpleasant smell of gasoline floating in the air. I flipped open the letter that had brought me out here. The paper was slightly weathered and beat from the many times that I had read it. It contained a handwritten note from my mother, reminding me to enjoy my time because it would not last forever. It reminded me to take a break from my tedious nine-to-five job in a cubicle, to “stop and smell the roses.” And so, standing in front of a magnificent view with the feeling of gritty sand at my feet, 20,000 miles from my apartment, I drew in another deep breath and vowed to truly live.
