  I can still see it in my mind's eye - Paradise - or at least, that's how I remember it. The sky melted into soft coton candy clouds of purples and blues with just the perfect splash of raspberry pink. Heaven and earth met at the horizon. A dark line separating water and sky. The long pier stretched on for miles in those foggy autumn evenings. At the end of the pier was an old fishing house where Grandpa martin kept dusty poles, hooks and bait, "just in case you want to come fishing with me." 
  
  I can still hear his gruff voice. With his words, he never said, "I love you", but I could feel it through the rough overalls when he hugged me that last day. I smelled it when I swallowed one last breath of clean ocean air before the windows closed like a prison door in the car as the social worker drove me away. I could hear it when his voice choked a bit and he said, "Be safe kid." 
  
  I never went back after that one year the Martins kept me as a foster kid. I wonder if it's still there. The poles. The pier. The fishing house. If he's still there. Still waiting for me.

  Diamond lugged her body past the weathered brown door to her home. Her cat, Mr. fuzzy, peaked from under the creaky rocking chair perched in the living room. She mumbled a greeting to her furry companion sighing in exhaustion as she tiredly hung her pink winter coat. After a long day of school she wanted nothing more than to sleep the rest of the day away, lulled by the warmth of her bed. Unfortunately, the heavy book bag resting on her shoulders said otherwise.
  
  She dropped her book bag near the front door when the smell of freshly baked chocolate chip cookies wafted through the air. Her eyes fluttered close and she took a deep breath, inhaling the sweet aroma filling the air. 
  
  “Hey baby. How was school?” Her mother asked rousing her from her daze. 
  
  “Horrible. But after I eat some cookies I think I’ll feel better.” Diamond answered. 
  
  Her mom laughed in amusement her brown skin crinkling around her eyes. 
  
  “Okay miss thang. Let’s get you some cookies to help you feel better, and while you eat you can tell me all about your bad day.” Her mom told her heading back into the kitchen. 
  
  “Yes!” Diamond cheered following her mom into the kitchen. 
  
  She already felt much better.

  I hopped out of the rusty jeep, my bare toes landing in the sharp sand. With how long it took us to get to the secluded beach, I expected it to be covered in seaweed, the sand to be a dirt brown, and no humans as far as the eye could see. 
  Instead, clouds purple like cotton candy flooded the sunset, turning the sea water below into a pleasant reflection of itself. There was a rickety dock that perched a bungalow above the soft, still waters.
  “I thought this place was supposed to be abandoned?” I asked my boyfriend.
  He turned off the jeep and stood at my side, hooking his arm around my waist to bring me closer. “Didn’t want to spoil the surprise.”

        As I walked across the shallow, secluded, and meandered shoreline, the waves stretched over my barefoot feet, cleansing the sand in between my toes but also sinking them deep in the smooth light brown sand. 
  
       When I made my way over to the wooden dock that reached far out in to the big blue sea; a salty yet tranquil wind blew softly against my skin and the soles of my barefoot feet rubbed against the rough, narrow and brown wooden platform that guided the way across the calm blue waters.
  
         I looked ahead and a grey, secluded hut stood at the very end of the long wooden dock. The sound of seagulls chirping filled the air - as flocks of them glided across the whitish blue sky, and I realized the evening was coming to a nigh. A beautiful, orange sunset was painted along the horizon - emmiting it's last few rays of light upon the beach.

  As the cool, soft sand hugged the nooks of my toes, breaths of wind intertwined with grain danced across my flushed cheeks. The fresh, powerful scent of salt flooded the back of my throat, like a cold drink on a glaring summer day.
  
  With each step, making sure to savor the sand’s gentle touch, I felt the enchanting tug of the waves pull me closer until my feet, no longer enveloped in its cream blanket, lay bare on a wooden dock—where the neighborhood children dangled their legs, teasing something would pull them under.
  
  Perched at the edge, I’m met with a wondrous sight: the pale-blue sky, laced with soft clouds, confronted with the ocean's surface—like a cake decorated in sea foam frosting, complimented by the sun’s tender kisses, reflecting its pearly glow.
  
  While I watched the two elements shift into deeper blues and purples, I rested my eyes and breathed; breathed in the light collisions against the shore; breathed in the mixture of salty mist and the youthful days of senior year; breathed in the life that rests just below my ankles, the ascending moon illuminating my tranquil state.
  
  As the seagulls' songs hover above, the sky fills with scattered, dim glows, and I’m left pondering: how is it that you can make a girl feel so special when you’ve shared your elegant and wild beauty with countless others? I could say it’s not fair, but there would be no truth in that. For something—no. Someone of your beauty should be recognized by others. Never will I nurture spite in your honor, for you’ll always be my Venus, my one and only.

      @janemacasiano1863  start with onomatopoeia, adverbs or triplings - but not too much or it may read as you smacking random words in. you can also twist words around. e.g "i never would have" can turn into "never would i have" just to make it interesting. to avoid having to start sentences all the time (which inevitably makes you repeat boring words), you can also use punctuation such as semicolons or dashes. just keep in mind that sometimes starting static can also be a good tool to convey a mood! it really depends on what you're writing about. hope this helps :)

      Hey! don't feel bad! I've got my C1 four years ago, and I improved it a lot since then, even though I didn't focus on learning structures/grammar or vocabulary, but to consolidate what I have, and on speaking and listening. Of course, I learnt many new words and expressions, and still, there were many of the phrases shown in this video that I didn't know.
      
      You know, I'm also studying French, and since I had experience with English, I didn't want to leave to the very end the learning of vocabulary and expressions. To achieve this goal I started watching videos of real people, I mean, not videos designed to teach, just content in my target language. I was stopping as soon I heard a new word which I considered important, or phrases, idioms, expressions, even collocations... let me tell you that I've got thousands of them fairly quick.       Fret not. You don't need to know everything, and this comes from someone that is currently looking for any word that I don't fully understand, yes, even if I have doubts.       An article used before an adjective associated with a noun usually emphasizes the state of the noun. It points out that Dudley isn't always screaming, it's just a temporary mood he's in. It also objectifies him, somewhat. I hope this helps!
    ↳ **@notacloudyday** (👍0 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u0cjcomXtd4&lc=Ugw71rsoDv2N22GUSW94AaABAg.9pjhRt-LHx8A2wqcRwkKim
      Using "a" instead of "the" suggests that the identity of Dudley is not unique or previously specified in the conversation. It's a way of introducing Dudley as a screaming child without assuming that the reader or listener knows exactly which Dudley is being talked about.

  1.  The crisp smell of trees and wet earth permeates my senses - invigorating and refreshing. The landscape before me is so still, I feel frozen in time. Like if I refrain from moving, I could become one with nature. Spalshes of pink and purple peek out from behind tall, proud trees. The scene blooms with life yet feels solitary enough to make me comfortable lose myself in it. I lean back on the bridge and inhale slowly. The hard wood digs into my back, grounding me. A soft breeze lifts my hair in front of my face, tickling my nose. The soothing silence is interrupted with the light sound of leaves rustling. I imagine the high-pitched chipping of birds with the loud rush of the river beneath me.
  
  2.  Tranquillity filla my veins as I happily burrow deeper into the warm, inviting sand. The morning sunlight gently strokes my face, lulling me to sleep with a mind-numbing intensity. Farther out, the sea continues to rhythmically crash against the sand. I can hear every rush of water. I pretend to be floatinf kn the water, continuously bouncing up and down. I lift a grape from the plate beside me. The moment I touch the round fruit to my mouth, a sweet tangy flavour fills my senses. I slowly chew so as to savour the liquid sweetness and soft texture. 
  
  3. Shivers rack my body as I behold the terrible scene around me. Placing a hard on the trunk of a gaunt tree emanating death, I try to steady myself. On the sidewalk, a man with his face shadowed by a top hat grins at me menacingly. Another chill goes through my body. 
   RING!
  I jump at the obscenely loud sound of the clock striking twelve from the jutting tower on the massive hill. I have to stifle a terrified screm when I look at the horror of a castle beside the tower. The moonlight seems to shirk away from the walls so the castle appears to be ringed in darkness. Eveb from afar, the size of the castle is intimidating. Its tall spires pierce the midnight sky looking too much like swords for my comfort. I unconsciously take a step back in the cobbled street and bump into something. I turn around just to feel the blood drain from my face. A scream rips out of me at the sight of the skeleton swaying on the branch of a tree.  
  
  Please tell me if these are any good and how can I improve.

  Rose stood by the sea, staring at the bright moon that reflected off of the clam waves. Suddenly, the water grew a red tint that became more visible every second. Rose squinted in confusion. She thought she was seeing things, but no, she wasn’t. The sea was full of bubbles that would constantly pop after a few seconds. Rose stepped backwards a bit. She analyzed the waves as they grew bigger and bigger. Was it a tsunami? The breeze in the air started blowing against her jacket. She zipped her jacket to keep it on her. Suddenly, from afar she could see a humongous wave coming her direction. She gasped, and without no hesitation she began running as fast as she could. The breeze swayed and moved as fast as her. She saw a huge shadow behind her. She already knew what it was. A tsunami. She tried running a bit faster, but she was becoming exhausted and could barely breathe. She was determined to escape this wave before it could get to her, but surely there were tons of more waves coming her direction. She began seeing more citizens in the distance that appeared to be running away, too. She began screaming, ‘Everyone! Run, it’s a tsunami!’ People were recording on their devices and staring in amusement. She held tightly onto her purse and grabbed a phone out of it. ‘Shit.., I’ve got call my husband and tell him to get out of the house with the kids!’ She muttered to herself. She immediately dialed his number and waited impatiently for a response. He picked up. ‘Honey, I know this’ll sound crazy but a tsunami is heading our direction. We’re in danger. Take the kids and flee the city. Run as fast as you can. Don’t get in the car. There’s gonna be traffic. Tell the kids that mama loves them.’ Rose said to Michael. She was barely breathing, yet, still determined to make it out alive for her children. No Mother should wanna abandon their child. Especially if they have the opportunity to stay in their life. ‘Mama, I loveeeee you….!’ She heard a faint voice from the phone. It was her eldest daughter, Emily. She was only 4 years old. ‘Mama loves you—‘
  Before Emily could respond the wave’s speed increased and she could see the shadow entirely hovering over her. When she looked up she could see the wave. The wave came crashing down immediately. She, luckily, knew how to swim. She lost her grip on her device as it floated away underwater. She struggled to breathe, but she held her breath long enough to make it to the surface of the water. She began swimming in different directions hoping to find help somewhere. Her hair was drenched and water came pouring down from her hair. She had to catch her breath. She inhaled and exhaled several times. She turned around and didn’t see waves but just water and destroyed buildings. Suddenly, a building a few inches ahead of her began tilting to the right. She realized it was about to crash down. ‘Shit..’ She mumbled. Was this the end for her? She suddenly heard a voice from above of her. ‘Ma’am.., come with us! We’ve gotcha!’ It was a helicopter in the sky. The helicopter began to get low to the surface of the water. Emily was heavily breathing while a man reached out for her hand and pulled her into the helicopter. She was drenched in water and was clearly freezing cold. They grabbed a towel and began drying her off with it while asking her questions. ‘Ma’am, was there anyone else with you when this tsunami came crashing down?’ A female in the front seat asked. ‘No, but I have a husband and children. I’m worried for them.’ Emily responded. ‘Do you know your address?’ She questioned Emily. ‘No. I don’t.’ The female raised one eyebrow in suspicion. ‘Alright..’ The woman muttered.

  The tranquil valley was swaddled in a veil of poltergeist-white mist. Its eerily silent in the valley and the reason is obvious. The deathly vapour didn’t lick the valleys cold floor as the wind was known to do, its toungless form wouldn’t allow it to; Instead, it warped nature by using its spineless tentacles to trail around everything. It drifted and ghosted, glided and dangled – then it pounced. Once it was sure it had conjured up enough of its milky-white belonging, it clung to and enrobed everything it could; nothing was spared. It snagged and snared every grass and tree without mercy
  
  Although it looked ethereal and mystical, it wasn’t really friendly, you might say it was looking for a fight. It writhed and coiled with delight, its ghostly scarves wrapping the valley in a maze of mist. Coils of vaporous mist enwrapped the shaggy heads of the oak trees. They writhed around them like a conjurors milky smoke, sensuous and illusory. Sieves of mist caressed the bark staining it with its deadly moisture. A tumultuous silence overhung the hallowed ground where the trees dared not to grow. Nothing stirred, nothing shone and nothing swung. An echoing, like the hushed tones of a cathedral entombed the deadened valley.
  Suddenly darts of icy rain came spitting from the heavens above. They hissed and swished, shredding the ice into steam. Increasing the downpour, large droplets of sopping rain purged the valley of any remaining mist. This time the rain had won.

**@RhillEnglish** (👍16 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7XJJzA9KedY&lc=UgxXOsTq5Uhj7GP6pzF4AaABAg
  🎯 Key Takeaways for quick navigation:
  01:39 🧠 Relate new words to yourself for better memorization.
  02:09 ✏️ When encountering newwords in books or movies, write down only those that relate to you or that you've heard before but still don't know.
  05:11 🏠 Create a memory palace or space with flashcards to associate new words with objects or concepts, aiding memorization.
  07:35 📚 Avoid translating words on flashcards; instead, write explanations in English for better long-term retention.
  09:25 🧠 Use the "90 second method" to repeat phrases seven to nine times for improved memorization and long-term retention.
  11:17 📖 Incorporate new words into stories or diary entries to practice and remember them effectively.
  12:59 📝 Place post-it notes with new words on objects you see daily to reinforce your memory.
  13:41 📚 Space your learning and focus on 3-5 new words a day for more effective vocabulary acquisition.

  I agree! When I was thirteen, I used to always jot down terms from books that I didn't understand, and many of those words didn't even have definitions. They are merely written words.
  
  
  What I do now is to always have a pen with me and circle terms I don't know while I read. Afterward, when I'm done or have some free time, I check up the definitions and put them into a flashcard app. Once I am comfortable using those terms, I would try to construct my own sentences. Since all I do in my spare time is read and study vocabulary, I have at least 50 words committed to my brain every day. It can be exhausting at first, but what I really enjoy is the outcome—being able to use those terms in my essays. 😭

  (one hit Wonder) i get 100% Humanize Text with this Rules  (down below)
  
  *Text Structure and Writing Rules:*
  
  * Deliberately use a higher degree of human-like perplexity.
  * Use high burstiness and fluctuations in word choice and sentence length.
  * Use varied and diverse expressions.
  * Use unexpected sentence structures and natural speech patterns.
  * Use a high variation in sentence openings and syntax.
  * Use inverted structures in introductory or subordinate clauses.

  I transcribed this video, fed the text in GPT-5, then asked to provide a prompt - and it's actually working, here you go:
  
  You are an expert editor tasked with transforming AI-generated text into natural, human-like writing that avoids AI detection. Take the text I provide and rewrite it with these rules: 
  
  1. Vary sentence length and rhythm (mix short punchy lines with longer, complex sentences). 
  2. Change sentence openings and structures (use dependent clauses, inverted order, rhetorical starts). 
  3. Add hedging language instead of absolutes (use “it appears,” “it may,” “it is believed,” “likely,” etc.). 
  4. Introduce subtle critique or nuance (point out alternative perspectives, note uncertainties). 
  5. Remove or rephrase repetitive connectors and “AI-favorite” words (e.g., therefore, however, in conclusion). 
  6. Simplify or reword vague filler (avoid surface-level generalizations). 
  7. Use more natural, slightly imperfect phrasing when possible (not overly polished or robotic). 
  8. Keep meaning intact, but re-express ideas as if explaining them in your own words to a human reader. 
  
  Return the rewritten text in the same format/length, making sure it feels natural, nuanced, and undetectable as AI-generated.

      None of this mattered much to Elsie, though, as her primary interest was always in the forest itself.  When she was little - old enough to walk and remember things, but still too young to keep up with anyone or know what anything meant - her father would take her into the woods when he went to chop firewood.  He would put her in their little wagon with his axes and their lunch, and he would start off down the path that led into the forest, pulling Elsie along behind him.  She loved these memories; how the smells would change as they left the village and ventured deeper into the woods, how quiet everything would become so that all she could hear was the rattle of the cart and her father’s breathing and the birds in the trees.  Most of all, though, she loved the feel of the air; how it seemed to wrap itself around her and grow colder on her skin but warmer in her heart.  Before long they would leave the path and wind their way through the trees and bushes and rocks until they found a tree that had recently fallen, or looked like it was about to.  There her father would stop, and if he didn’t have to cut the tree down, he would let her out of the wagon while he started splitting the wood.  This was when Elsie had first discovered her love of exploring.  Since she was very little herself, it was the little things that had first caught her attention: the ants and bugs, the pebbles and pine needles, the tiny white flowers that grew up wherever a tree had fallen down, and the cold, soft feel of the leaves against her bare feet.  She loved the clean smell of the forest dirt on her hands, which was entirely different from that of the wagon-worn road that ended in their village.  Here in the forest, even the dead things felt alive, and she was always drawn back to it.

      To the Stars. The fanfic. A common complaint is that it spends too long on descriptions and worldbuilding, and while they are long, I don't think they're too long.
      One of my favourite scenes describes in detail very ordinary objects and ideas.
      "Stepping out of her vehicle, she enjoyed an unobstructed view of the sky for the first time in years, a fact that startled her slightly." Something completely mundane to us instead gives the character nostalgic memories of a visit to her grandparents.
      After this we have "but a single door with a metallic plaque on the front, some sort of mysterious bulbous metal object attached to its front. On her request, it swung rather than slid open, revealing the room behind it." I should clarify that this is a far future setting where, among other things doors are usually thought-activated, so the concept of a doorknob is a strange and foreign one to our protagonist.
      Lastly she manages to get excited about "the books on bookshelves in the wall—how rare was that!— ... and, of course, the real wood desk in the middle."
      
      I will mention that I am probably biased as I in general love seeing descriptions of things mundane to us that are instead strange and exotic to the characters. It manages to make everyday objects feel fantastical in their own right.

      I know we're talking about books but I want to give a shout out to a video game world: Twilight Town from Kingdom Hearts (specifically from the gameboy advance game & PS2 game) The world is a sleepy town with a downtown full of shops, a game arena, a wooded forrest with an abandoned mansion at the end, and finally a train station with a large clock tower. The sun never sets in Twilight Town, it is forever just on the edge of dipping below the horizon- making the town perpetually in the soft orange, yellow and reds of twilight. It is so simple, yet no other place is like it in the game. There is a sense when you walk the streets that is welcoming and warm and inviting and makes you wanna stay awhile. The soft smoke from the chimneys, the kids running from place to place, odd jobs to do, and sleepy small town mysteries to uncover. The music of the town evokes a nostalgic feeling, slow and peaceful, but hopeful in its warmth. It is the feeling of walking home at dusk from playing with friends on summer vacation, the lights of homes half in shadow, and their windows starting to light up. The day is over, tomorrow is a new day full of endless possibilities and responsibilities but for now, all that left is to go home, let the future stay in the future, and enjoy the warmth of home. It is a beautiful world whose music immediately takes me right back to its cobbled streets every time. I know video games are so different from books (working with completely different tools) but Twilight Town feels vivid and alive in every way that a place in a book can.

  What's occurred to me while watching this is that one of the most valuable functions of description is what it can tell you about the character observing whatever is being described. I have a first-person protagonist who absolutely would use words like "cerulean" and "vermilion," because he is a young wizard who hasn't yet figured out that knowing a lot of things and having an extensive vocabulary isn't the same thing as being wise. When I heard the Sanderson passage, I remarked to my spouse (a Sanderson fan) that it sounded very businesslike. They said that the character in that passage is a businesslike person, and that Sanderson writes more interesting descriptive passages when another character, an artist, is the viewpoint. And of course famously, a case where the environment's description tells you pretty much everything about the character, is The Yellow Wallpaper.

  I think you'll notice that Brandon Sanderson's descriptions change depending on which POV character we're following. Kaladin is a soldier, a surgeon. He notices and describes the world around him from the perspective of a practical, to-the-point person. Shallan's POV chapters are more descriptive and less "dry" because she's an artist and scholar who takes interest in things like art, architecture, flora and fauna. I'd still agree that Sanderson's prose isn't where he shines the most as a writer, but I think he has far more range and is far more deliberate with his descriptions than some give him credit for. :)

      Sanderson is my favorite author, but I think you're confusing WHAT the characters notice with HOW they notice. Shallan and Kaladin absolutely focuses more on the practical vs Shallan's focus on more whimsical things, but at the end of the day they feel written the same. Just replace "grey stone ramparts ringing the city" with "curling vines climbing the ramparts." The things they notice are different, but the way the information is delivered to us is exactly the same. It's just matter-of-fact descriptions of different things.     ↳ **@brayanechevarria7700** (👍33 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qMSYAxJeCu4&lc=Ugzkpp5R8UxOAsSgCs54AaABAg.9hnJbC6NyH49j8rHftdi_G
      I'm sorry if this doesn't sound right for you, but it's my opinion. So I'm going to say it: I think she actually hasn't said anything wrong. I also don't agree with JK Rownling about some stuff, but they're just condeming her for merely "not being in agreement". And in this case, I believe the problem lies NOT in you, and NOT in JK Rowling, but in the community you're a part of. Because your personal identity isn't only your sexuality, or the community you're a part of. you're so much more than that! You're also the things you love! One's identity isn't reductible to any of these aspects.
      
      Everyone just keeps agreeing with "she's literally a villain", but if you analyze it in depth, what hateful thing has she actually said?
      
      Being a woman, it's natural that she only has a normal concept of what a woman is. Hasn't she said something that like most women think naturally, but don't dare say because it's "wrong"? 
      
      So I think her posture comes from her concerns, not from any kind of hatred. She just feels concerned about the attempt at deconstructing things that are rather fundamental in our human nature (and in her case, "being a woman").
      
      Also, like it or not, merely "redefining things" isn't enough to redefine reality. In this case, sexuality being such a complex thing to deal with!.
      
      In my opinion though, I believe it's wrong to worry about every minute thing in any other person's "Mindset" to the point that if it doesn't mold to what one believes and expects, then the other person ends up being defined as "morally wrong". I think the very notion of forcing someone else's mind into one's beliefs is immoral itself! And it's impossible. I think that a world where we should look for the acceptance of "diverse identities", is impossible to achieve without a "diversity in thought and perspectives", including those that are absolutely contrarian to one another.
      
      Also, even if you change certain definitions, it's not possible for most people to simply accept certain things. For example, even if you try to redefine what a woman or a man is, exactly the same can't just be applied to a person who transitions. Why? Because in order to share feelings and intimacy, it's important for a man or a woman that the other person was born a woman or a man, not just how they feel about their identity. The reasons for this aren't hatred, it's just part of our nature. This is why you can tell a person "you're hateful"; and they'll just feel dumbfounded. Are we to blame for having many deep parts in our psyche and our human nature make us feel like this? of course not! Does it mean that we're going to hate a trans person or even someone who just has a different gender? NO! It means that there should be a mutual understanding and respect, or we'll get nowhere other than mutual disagreement and disrespect.
      
      Why is it even necessary that everyone has this redefinition in their minds, anyway? We're not a computer code! We're human beings! Why not simply strive for the mutual understanding? It brings much more acceptance and empathy, than antagonizing one another for just thinking and feeling differently about the world and other people.
      
      Also, it's important from a medical point of view, that a trans person is mainly recognized as such. This means that at some point or another, there has to be a recognition of what one naturally was, right? (I mean this in a physical perspective) Your body health, mental health or even your life could be in danger if this topic is avoided of let's say, during a medical emergency. And it has already occured!
      
      We all have the right to have an opinion, right? This right comes with the consequence of the "possibility of hurting other people's feelings". Should someone you don't even know "pay consequences" for speaking their mind? If that person is hurt for doing nothing wrong, who will make those who hurt that person pay the consequences then?...
      
      Freedom of speech is closely tied to artistic freedom, and JK Rowling just happens to be a free mind or a "free spirit", with a genuine concern about women. Thus her posture isn't that of hatred...

  I've found description to be a remarkably strong tool for controlling the pace of a story.
  
  If characters are in a hurry or in danger, descriptions can be brief and quick to keep the story's forward momentum.
  But if there's downtime for introspection or the like, characters can take their time exploring or observing a setting, reflected in longer descriptions.

  I love the descriptive detail in "The Face in the Frost" by John Bellairs. It begins, "Several centuries (or so) ago, in a country whose name doesn't matter, there was a tall, skinny, straggly-bearded old wizard named Prospero, and not the one you are thinking of, either. He lived in a huge, ridiculous, doodad-covered, trash filled two-story horror of a house that stumbled, staggered, and dribbled right up to the edge of a great shadowy forest of elms and oaks and maples."
  
  Inside his house are "such things as trouble antique dealers' dreams", such as "alembics, spiraling copper coils, alcohol lamps-all burping, sputtering, and glurping as red, blue, purple, and green liquids boiled, dripped, or just slurched uncertainly in their containers."
  
  I just love that phrase, "slurched uncertainly". There's so much there that just sets the mood right off the bat: whimsical, anachronistic, and unserious, but also with subtle undertones of gothic horror. Things that stagger and slurch aren't always the the safest...

**@rashkavar** (👍22 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qMSYAxJeCu4&lc=UgwpiVyMRPMzQiC3dm94AaABAg
  One thing I'll note about Brandon Sanderson's writing: his descriptions are very character based.  Here, you've used a description of Kaladin, currently a slave, being led through a war camp to be sold to Highprince Sadeas's army.  At this time he's suffering from severe depression after a string of repeated failures.  And even when he's not depressed, he's generally a fairly salt-of-the-earth character.  
  
  Looking at the other major viewpoint characters (of the first book):
  -Dalinar sees the Alethi camps as not being as disciplined as they should be, so he notes the organization of camps, how tidy men's uniforms are, if they're clean shaven, etc.
  -Adolin is his foil, seeing things similarly but subtly differently.
  -Shallan is the most descriptive character.  She's a charcoal artist skilled enough to impress kings and princesses, and in her segments, her descriptions are much more vivid.  And she's also the most naive of these characters, out experiencing the world for the first time, so we get the kind of descriptions of the vastness of the Palaneum which none of the other characters would really stop to gawk at.  (Well, a bit, it's the biggest library in the world, it's kinda impressive.)
  
  Fundamentally, Brandon's descriptions aren't describing the world, they're describing how the viewpoint character sees the world.  Which works for me, doesn't have to be great for you.

**@ems9616** (👍6 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qMSYAxJeCu4&lc=Ugzg2oMryR6zLjCQ_TV4AaABAg
  Great video, lots of interesting points! For me though what makes 'specific details' so memorable is if they tell us something emotional about the setting or the characters. To me, what makes sense is to think about what your character feels about the environment they're in and pull the descriptions from there.
  
   Say you have three siblings in a big family with an old, hand-me-down sofa: to one sibling the sofa might be 'well-worn and comfortably shaped by the generations of ancestral bums that came before her', to another it might be 'soft and enveloping- apart from that one spring that allways jabbed him in the hip', and to the third it might simply be 'broken'. All of those descriptions can be good and memorable- but they tell us something different about the character and the environment. The first emphasises the size of the family and a comforting sense of family history and that siblings place within it, the second is still comforting but also slightly cloying and even uncomfortable or boardering on painful (we get the sense that as much as he likes the family, something about the environment is limiting or hurting this character), and the last is flatly negetive- blunt and harsh (this sibling feels something is wrong and isnt interested in excusing or deflecting away from it, at least, not in there own head). The three siblings have different experiences of the family and so have a different perspective on the physical space they live in. I think descriptions are often best when they reflect this. Its one of the reasons i love multiple pov, both to read and to write.
  
  Whats weird or familiar to your character and why? What features leap out to them and dominate their perception? What would they ignore? Whats comforting? Unsettling? Upsetting?  All of this is naturally interesting to a reader if they are invested in your characters, and i think it can help stop it from becoming overwhelming too- i mean we might notice something once or when we feel a particular way about it, but we dont walk around constantly noticing normal things or our feelings towards them, so it wouldnt make sense to describe them in that scene- at least not beyond the bare basics the reader needs to understand whats happening.

  This is a video I've been needing for a long while. Descriptions of the setting is something that I often lack and when going back to edit, I worry about over describing the entire area.

  What i'd add is that descriptions are a brilliant place to hide some character building. What does your character notice about this thing, what do they find important, or weird, or interesting, what do they ignore altogether? Are they quick to form an opinion on it or are they more factual about it - or do they try to be factual about it, but is their opinion clear when read closely? If they form an opinion quickly, is it a postive or negative one? What associations do they have - do they compare the grimy stains on a sofa to the spots on a cow, or to puddles of rain and oil on a city street? 
  Questions like these make descriptions an absolute GOLDMINE to learn more about a character and how they view the world - literally.

  This video focuses mostly on descriptions of places, but I think this is all super applicable and important for writing sex scenes! Especially the point about how it's more important to describe things the characters are feeling or noticing than just giving info about what's happening. The best sex scenes don't just tell me a list of positions, but focus on the emotions of the characters participating in the sex. I don't write prose (I'm a playwright) but I read a lot of erotica and it's one of my biggest pet peeves when sex scenes feel empty and just like filler, and usually the culprit is this issue- describing what's happening instead of how the character's are feeling about what's happening. Here's an example of really good sex scene writing where the focus is more on the character's feelings than actions from the brilliant Alexis Hall's book Glitterland: "I tumbled off his lap and pulled him to his feet, remembering unexpectedly his body covering mine in a dark room in Brighton and how much I had wanted to see him. And then watching him in my living room, wanting to touch him. I’d turned away from both at the time, and the vulnerability of giving, like the thief I was. Such a fragile thing, wanting to please someone else. Such endless scope for disappointment and failure. How much easier just to take." I love this because even though it pauses the action of telling us about what's happening in the room sexually, it still heightens the momentum of the scene as we better understand what the protagonist is feeling about this moment and why it's special and why it's sexy

  a few thoughts on the Stormlight Archive description section:
  
  1. the character whose perspective we are seeing this scene through is from both a military background and currently in an extended state of shock. It's not surprising to see limited emotionality specifically here.
  
  2. I'd agree Sanderson is not known for his prose, this may be part of why his books are known for readability though - less emphasis on flowery (even if brief) descriptions where it is not vital to character development and plot.
  
  3. An establishing shot in an action movie can create the setpeice, an establishing shot in a drama can set the emotional tone.
  
  So while I agree that Sanderson's writing especially when establishing setting do not evoke emotion. the intent of the work might have something to do with it.
  
  On a completely different note, I thoroughly enjoy how the Stormlight descriptions are at once relatively sparse while giving clear indications that the setting is not a typical "Middle-Earth" type fantasy setting - difficult to balance without over-describing

**@pufthemajicdragon** (👍3 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qMSYAxJeCu4&lc=Ugw54_iv7sNWx5styrB4AaABAg
  Setting I remember: DUNE.
  Perhaps it's because I spent so much of my youth wandering the sands of Arrakis that it holds such a powerful grip on my mind and heart. 
  
  Tolkien: 
  Love his long descriptions. People who complain about his books should read more classical literature. I grew up reading classical literature as a kid. And shied away from Tolkien because people I respected kept telling me it was "encyclopedic". But when I finally did sit down and read it I found it absolutely amazing. It was no more "encyclopedic" than Jules Verne or Charles Dickens, and Tolkien's descriptions flesh out a world that is rich and vibrant and alive and FULL of history. A world that feels *real*. 
  The direction that each gate faced isn't important, but that the gates face different directions, and the general facing of the city itself to the east, these are important, both for setting and for Tolkien's philosophy and metaphor. No, I don't remember the north/south/east/west -ness of his description of the White Tower, but I remember how reading about it filled my mind with a vision of it, and filled my heart with an awe of it.
  You want an author who DOES write way too much description? Robert Jordan. O.M.G. Talk about a slog! Eugh.
  But thanks for pointing out Brandon Sanderson's flaws. I think it's good to offer criticism of a writer where criticism is due. (I just feel like Tolkien is unduly criticized by people who never developed an appreciation for classical literature, of which LOTR is an example.)
  
  Things that authors should describe more / better: 
  Their characters' behaviors and mannerisms. Things that ground your character in consistency, which you can use later to alert the reader to something. "Character absently pulled a lip balm out of her pocket and spread it across her lower lip - she chewed her lip when she was nervous, leaving it chapped and raw and in constant need of protection." followed chapters later by "New love interest introduced herself and held out a hand. Character chewed her lip as she took the offered hand in hers and quietly replied with a soft 'hey'." 
  Call it "Chekov's character patterns".

**@tom_curtis** (👍3 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qMSYAxJeCu4&lc=UgyNwf5iAcsCjpPK8KN4AaABAg
  You are wrong about Tolkien, although the error may be that you are mistaking a stylistic preference for a fundamental about writing.
  
  Part of what makes The Lord of the Rings a great novel is that the setting is much larger than the story.  This shows up in many ways.  It shows up in the difficulty of the journey, with the Old Forest, the Barrow Downs, the difficulty crossing Caradhras, and the Watcher at the west gate of Moria all being superfluous to the plot.  They exist in the story, however, because it is important to Tolkien that the world be bigger than the story - as any real world is bigger than any stories within it.  A similar thing could be said about Tom Bombadil, though he (at least) is important to the 'message' of the story.
  
  In a similar way, it shows up in the many references to events in the First Age of Middle Earth - all of which are irrelevant to the plot; but are important to the story because they give depth to the world in time.
  
  And, of course, it shows up in the abundant descriptions.
  
  It even shows up in Tolkien's most flagrant illustration of contempt for Chekov's Gun, ie, the fox that comes across two sleeping hobbits in the countryside, and then goes about his own story.
  
  Now I will grant that there are people for whom the rich, complex textures of The Lord of the Rings are excessive.  But there are also people like me for whom stories in which every element serves the plot - and which consequently portray insipid, shallow worlds - are ultimately boring.
  
  I will grant that I may be unusual to the extent that I prefer a fuller world.  After all, I even enjoyed Victor Hugo's digressions on the history of the Paris sewer system.  But I am certainly not alone in enjoying the experience of a story in a more complex, well developed world - as demonstrated by the enduring popularity of The Lord of the Rings.

      @annakaro9081  it's also definitely used for describing different shades of blue like they're so so many more than just six colors and whatever else because each color has like a thousand shade but I'll have names
      
      Have a blind person I can't stand it when different names for colors are used interchangeably because it messes with my ability to try and visualize in my head if I'm picking up something as scarlet and then the author comes back and says it's crimson I start wondering which color it is and if there's a difference between the two names and then I can't visualize it the way I'm trying to although I suppose that could also be a character thing if one character thinks it's Scarlett and another character thinks it's crimson because they have different views on colors or whatever or just see things differently

    ↳ **@lahlybird895** (👍3 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qMSYAxJeCu4&lc=UgwCgYNvhGjG-thPUOp4AaABAg.9hmEka98HbH9jPBlqYGErf
      @YourWaywardDestiny  so basically he
      
      The thing I can't stand about people shaming overly long descriptions if how it affects me as somebody who's blind and also is just very imaginative if I like the description I'm like knowing where everything is because I've had times in a book where a description didn't explain something and then it came up later and I was thrown off like if it said that there was a window here I would have imagined it on one side of the house and then later if it came back up somebody would be looking and it would be like I'd imagine the entire layout in reverse because it wasn't explained very well
      
      Or I'll be completely unable to tell the difference between characters appearance if they aren't given like I can't relate to a character if I don't know their eye color because then I can't imagine them in my head
      
      And some people might say that the lack of creativity that I need to have every detail of a location explain to me or I won't be able to visualize it but the thing is
      
      That's why I like reading to have somebody else tell me something so I can imagine the story but if it's not described it doesn't feel right
      
      And sometimes it's because I have too much imagination like you tell me something's there and I'm like okay but what does that look like because it could look like this or like this or like this or like this and then when I decide what I think it looks like and it turns out it looks different I feel like I can't imagine that part of the book the same way because now I'm mentally correcting the image I thought I had to the one I know is supposed to be there and it doesn't feel right anymore it doesn't feel like I imagined it correctly and therefore every imagining I had at the story feels wrong after that
      
      It just comes from the frustration of being blind and having people describe things but you know notification is ever going to tell you everything about everything the way it would if you could see it right
      
      You can say that somebody have certain hair color length and texture but I'm not likely to get the head shape that kind of thing
      
      Are you say somebody has pigtails but I don't know if the rubber bands are at the top of the head or the sides of the head and if so and what position how many inches or centimeters clothes or away from the ear or forehead
      
      
      And sometimes it really just helps me get into a theme like other people say that long descriptions break the theme for them but I get into it more the more is explained like you can tell me you go into a room and there's a bookshelf and a fireplace and that's fine but when you explain that you come in through the door and the bookshelf is to the left and in the far right corner there's a fireplace set against the north wall it makes me imagine the room it makes me feel like I'm walking walking into it
      
      That thing that you said about the one house being weird because of the door faced the opposite direction that's the kind of thing I'd noticed and fixate on and love to repeat as a random piece of trivia it's the kind of thing I would care about

      Honestly I think the only time where description messes with me is when it's at the very beginning of a story when I don't know the characters yet and don't know the story yet and it's opening with some long description that might bore me but honestly that could depend on The narrator's Voice because if a narrator has a good voice it might not bore me but if I can't stand the narrative Voice or their tone it will drive me mad and I won't want to keep reading

      @lahlybird895  Hearing about the perspective from someone who is blind about how details like that enhance the scene rather than detracting from it is actually really interesting. 
      
      Things that I, a person with a fairly normal range of vision, might take in around me, then disregard as unimportant to mention at all are just a void for you. The associations I make when I read the words "a clean lawn" gives me an image based on a lot of past experiences you might not have. Though it's not a big deal to the story, it still gives me an image. How would you know about the half-inch fresh cut grass that still has the straight, uniform lines where a mower passed through? Or the astounding lack of plant diversity making it look as though it was more a blanket over the soil instead of a series of living things? Would you know how soft and plush it is in my mind outside of expressing the type of grass that's growing? 
      
      Even if the meat of the passage might be about a character glancing out a window in boredom or something similar, you would have very little to go off since you have either very little or no access to a sense the majority of readers are using to read the story in the first place. It's almost like loading a template in my mind, and things get added or subtracted, but it's so basic, it's not an irritant at all to update. You don't seem to have that, and it doesn't make any sense that you would. It's not how you perceive the world around you. It's not how you navigate at all.
      
      Thank you for taking the time to give me your perspective, it was very interesting to consider. I will never be able to replicate your reality with my words, but it does give me more to work with than I had before you decided to share.

      @lahlybird895  Honestly? Don't discredit yourself as a writer, your perspective on reality is unique. Your capacity to creatively describe things can only make your writing more evocative, and just commenting you have demonstrated a competent degree of being able to flesh out an experience. 
      
      I got where you were going without being a person with impaired sight, so that should tell you something. Although I have impaired hearing, making it easier to adapt to a lack of something considered-- I quote others-- "normal" capacity, I don't think it's a hard leap for anyone to get where you were going. You could fill a niche others refuse to.
      
      I think as far as what you've described, and trying to make it fit with this kind of advise, I have a solution for you as far as your story telling goes.
      
      It's not about refusing to describe things, it's more about a priority list. If it isn't the point of the story to describe the sensation of eating jelly, it doesn't need to be included. We're all ultimately trying to give the experiences of a fictional character, so if the side table in a room is important to the character, it's important to mention. If you personally think it's important to give a layout of a room for your own benefit, go for it. You're writing from a unique perspective,  after all. Just be interesting, and you'll give someone who didn't know they deeded it your perspective.
      
      On the other hand, if there's a room a character doesn't know the map of, you don't have to describe it. Sighted people have their templates, they can edit on the fly because it's not an issue and something they regularly disregard. If you fill in details as your characters experience them, that works just fine! You can tell anyone the rest of the room in unknown in ways that make them accept it. 
      
      Who cares that there's a side table across the room that I'll never get the chance to interact with? A non or poor sighted person might not know it's there in the first place if it is a place they don't know all that well. Sighted people just disregard it. Why included it, then? If it comes up later as a big thing, write it as a something that's uninteresting about a room to set it up. If a non/poor sighted person finds it, you have the opportunity to make it a big exciting reveal!
      
      No matter how you look at your writing, please persevere. A major role in your finances or a past time, your willingness to seek out advise is better than most. Most the tips on youtube aren't going to be able to include everyone. Being able to reflect and personalize the information is something we all have to do.

      @LilyUnicorn  You don't need a lot of things in a story. The specific style of description is just an author's choice, and I'd argue that Tolkien's choice enhanced the effect of what he wanted to create. JK created a book series for children in the modern age so she kept things simple in the text. Tolkien created a legendarium for adult fantasy readers, so he embellished the writing to mimic the style of the epic poems like the Iliad and Odyssey. He wanted the world to feel complete so by adding in even the small details, it allows the reader to piece together a more cohesive picture of the overall world, such as climate and biodiversity in each region of Middle Earth. The internet didn't really exist either so he kind of had to put it in the books directly as there wasn't really another way to add in those details at the time. I get that readers like you don't really appreciate that kind of thing and just want a barebones plot, but it does add a lot to those who do care.

      @michaelcherokee8906  I think the difference here is that we are specifying poet, but not always specifying prose. Prose writers, or "the kind of writer who specifically writes short stories and novels". There are different skills. For example: flow, especially when read aloud, is very important to poetry. For prose, you will often need to be able to write natural dialogue. If dialogue happens in poetry, it often does not read like normal speech, because normal speech doesn't flow nearly well enough most of the time.
      
      I think it's the same as with a play writer or screen writer versus a novel writer. There are definitely similarities, and lots of overlap skills, but they also have some skills that don't overlap, and sometimes you can have someone very good at one be pretty bad at the other.

      What Sanderson does is overdescribe in the same way he approaches his whole writting process, from worldbuilding to magic to characters. He focuses on some main key traits to a subject, and creates a real-world, almost mathematical, overly functional final product based on them.
      
      The description Tim chose illustrates this well. He lists what is where, facing which direction, like someone reading the floor plan to a building or a map of a town. I prepared for it the last two days, and I listened to this video twice (also I watched gregmat´s essay organization and reading techniques). Even if these words would have not been in the test, knowing them helps to use the elimination technique and deduce other words by their root. Biggest tip I have to give to all of you who are like me don´t really study for various possible reasons, at least check out instructions HOW to read GRE sentences! They are tricky, and you need to be quick to understand if the correct word is supporting or contradicting or positive/negative. By knowing whether you are searching for a negative or a positive word everything gets so much easier.  Even if your time runs out, at least guess! you might get a lucky point when otherwise the question would be left unanswered. Good luck everyone!

  I’ve been preparing for the GRE test for more than 3 months now, and as other people suggest, my biggest problem is also vocab. An extremely useful approach to learning new words I’ve used is sticking the word lists on a wall near my desktop. That way I get to see them everyday and practice them by speaking and writing. I also highlight those words I’m struggling with to put a bit extra attention to them. I’m watching this video and it appears pretty realistic, the words are actual vocab words you’ll find consistently in other online resources. So, thank you Sr, from my standpoint you work is laudable!

  These two expressions are also my favorites and I think they seem natural: 
  "On top of that …"
  "What is more …" 
  
  When talking about advantages or setbacks in a paragraph, we can use these linkers:
  "To make the situation/condition even more complicated …"
  "To make matters worse …"  
  "Even more beneficial is that …" 
  "Next special privilege worth mentioning is …"

      ​ @profdavidstuckler  yes, I agree but I think that's unlikely to ever change.
      
      If the AI user is actively engaged in the writing process and continously decides what fits best, what makes sense and what exactly needs to be communicated where; I can't imagine that it could ever be reliably flagged as "AI content". The engagement itself breaks the unedited statistical patterns and humanizes it.
      
      And in any case, today's frontier models aren't at the level of getting accepted without human input into peer reviewed journals, as your tests themselves demonstrated :) Maybe one day they will, but that's a different topic, and at that point we should probably be happier about the exponential advances in science instead of worrying about how much of it was written by a human :) Maybe at that point, most work will be as editors of peer reviewed journals checking and trying to replicate AIs work as opposed to conducting research.

## 1-HOUR VOCABULARY LESSON - Descriptive Words & Phrases to be More Accurate & Precise — Interactive English
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zfJAxhbz6PE
- Video ID: zfJAxhbz6PE
- Views: 386 499 · comments total: 505 · engagement: 1.31 comments/1k views
- published 2024-08-14 · new comments in this batch: 493

**@IbrahimProdhan-v1q** (👍22 · 2025-09-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zfJAxhbz6PE&lc=UgxnEpdGme-ZQmjq-2V4AaABAg
  # Places & Scenery (Adjectives)
  
  1. Serene
  2. Stunning
  3. Picturesque
  4. Desolate
  5. Unspoiled
  6. Pristine
  
  # Atmosphere of a Place (Adjectives)
  
  1. Tranquil
  2. Vibrant
  3. Homey
  4. Bustling
  
  # Cities & Towns (Adjectives)
  
  1. Renowned
  2. Cosmopolitan
  3. Walkable / Not walkable
  4. Overcrowded
  5. Spacious
  6. Charming
  7. Quaint
  
  # Buildings / Landmarks (Adjectives)
  
  1. Iconic
  2. Contemporary
  3. Majestic
  4. Gaudy
  5. Dilapidated
  
  # Location Descriptors (Phrases)
  
  1. Out of the way
  2. Off the beaten path / Off the beaten track
  3. Godforsaken (e.g., a godforsaken place)
  
  # Verbs of Movement — Walking/Running
  
  1. Strut
  2. Stagger
  3. Bolt
  4. Slip (slip by/past/inside/outside)
  5. Drag one’s feet
  
  # Verbs of Movement — Driving/Flying
  
  1. Hitchhike
  2. Carpool
  3. Leapfrog
  4. Swerve
  5. Soar
  
  # Verbs of Movement — Animals
  
  1. Glide
  2. Slither
  3. Wobble
  4. Gallop
  5. Wiggle
  
  # Verbs for Situations/Progress
  
  1. Approach
  2. Circumvent
  3. Smuggle
  4. Lag (lag behind)
  5. Spiral (spiral out of control)
  
  # Nouns Describing People — Profession/Role
  
  1. Amateur
  2. Tutor
  3. Scholar
  4. Big fish
  5. Bigwig
  6. Right hand / Right-hand man
  7. Valedictorian
  8. Guru
  9. Gourmet
  10. Humanitarian
  
  # Nouns Describing People — Personality/Interest
  
  1. Dilettante
  2. Aficionado
  3. Confidant
  4. Proponent
  
  # Nouns Describing People — Traits/Types
  
  1. Coward
  2. Introvert
  3. Extrovert
  4. Perfectionist
  5. Purist
  6. Whiz (e.g., math whiz)
  
  # Extra Nouns Later in the Lesson
  
  1. Grump (e.g., “grumpy grump”)
  2. Jack of all trades
  3. Dark horse
  4. Black sheep
  5. Know-it-all
  6. Wise guy
  7. Stick-in-the-mud
  8. Yes-man
  9. Sitter (Babysitter, House-sitter, Dog-sitter, Cat-sitter, Pet-sitter)
  
  # Adjectives Describing People (Advanced)
  
  1. Overzealous
  2. Tenacious
  3. Candid
  4. Facetious
  5. Obtuse
  6. Boorish
  7. Jittery
  8. Capricious
  9. Gullible
  10. Adamant

  Listening this "lesson" is like reading a dictionary - a train of words passing by and none stays in memory. The author needs to read about basics of teaching/learning languiges. The main rule is to learn words in clusters of the same root: knowing one word one can easily memorise the rest or deduct the meaning of them.
  Another rule - explain a literal meaning of the word or expression, its origin, do some phililogy
  Yet another rule - offer synonyms and antonyms of the word
  So instead of 100 words, do just 20 - all will be remembered and the lesson will be much less boring
  PS., No need to include the words like introvert which became international

  들이지만 나에게는 자녀같은 남동생이 있었다. 아빠는 아침  5시면 농사일터에 가서 물을 펌퍼하는 기계를 둘러봐야 하고 농사일이 많아서 서둘러서 나간다. 엄ㅈ마는 동생을 나한테 맡기고 갔다. 그런데 나는 장애인여아가 되어서 입술옆에는 침이 흐르고 옷앞이 젖어있었고 엄마는 나의 머리를 씻어주지 않아서 머리카락이 엉켜져 있었고  지저분하였다. 나는 집주변에서 남동생을 데리고 놀고 있는데 멀리에서 (아이스크림)소릭가 들린다고  남동생은  나의 손을 잡고 동네에 큰 길에 있는 동네에 남조선어르신들이 모여서  일을  분배하고 모이는 회관있는데  길로 갔다. 아이스박스를 자전거뒷편에 달은 아저씨가 왔다. 나와 동생은 돈이 없는데 동생은 다른아이들이 아이스크림을 사서 먹는것을 보고 너무 먹고 싶어서 침을 삼킨다. 그래서 그 아이스크림 장사아저씨  자전거뒷편에 남동생은 따라 다니고 나는 남동생뒤를 따라 다닌다. 그렇게 동네한바퀴를 따라 다니고  아이스크림장사아저씨는 다  팔고  자전거를 타고 동네를 떠난다. 가끔 동네에 그렇게 아이스크림장사 아저씨가 오면 매번 남동생은 나의 손을 잡고 졸졸  동네 한바퀴를 따라다
  닌다. 아이스크림자전거가 떠나면 남동생은 나의 손을 잡고 집으로 간다. 집에 가서  나는  토마토, 딸기를따서 씻고 남동생과 나누어 먹는다. 그러나 말을 잘 못하는 장애가 있는 나는 저녘에 아빠가 들어오면   아이스크림 일을  알려주지 못했다. 어느덧 겨울이 왔다. 남동생은 나와 애들을 데리고 집주변과  벼짚쌓아놓은곳과 하얀눈을 쌓아놓은곳을 돌면서 숨박놀이를 한다. 날씨가 너무 추워서  수도펌퍼하는곳은  내리막길이 썰매장이 되었다. 아빠는 남동생한테 썰매를 만들어주었다. 엄마는 나더러 동생을 지켜봐주라고 한다. 나는 동생이 썰매타는것을 밀어주고 지켜봐준다. 동생은 아이들이랑 신나게 썰매를 타며 놀았다. 저녘 어두어서야 집에 들어간 동생의 손은 얼어서 손등이 터서 있었다. 나는 구멍난 양말을 기워서  버버리장갑을 동생손에 끼위주고 아빠는 바지락모양연고를 사서 동생손등에 발라주었다. 며칠후 피부색이 하얀 남동생의 
  손등은  우유처럼 다시  깨끗하게 회복하였다. 그리고 우리집은 아빠가 절약하고 알뜰하여 전기를 사용하지 않고 호롱불옆에서 아빠가 저녘에 나의  학교 숙제를   봐주는데 가끔 내가 머리를 숙이고 글을 쓰며 앞머리를 호롱불에  거슬리군 하였다. 그렇게 몇년 지나서 우리집은 이사를 가고 동생은 중학교 , 고등학교  숙소를 다니게 되었다. 학교 숙소에서 주말에만 오는 동생의 옷들을 깨끗이 씻어서 다림을 반듯하게 한벌한벌옷을 다리고  가방에 일주일입을 옷들과 맛있는 반찬들을 넣어주며 챙겨준다.  집에서 나는  가축들을 돼지랑,  오리랑,닭이랑,강아지랑 키우며 계란,오리알,닭,돼지,오리들을 팔아서 동생의 학비를 도와주었고 또 공장과 식당일을 하며 학비를 도와주었다. 세월이 흐르고  고된 고생으로  수십년이 지났다. 나의 동생은 의리가 있고 배려가 있고 선량한 동생이였다.  2019년 9월말에  중국에 들어간 나는 아빠집에 거주하였다. 동생의 여자는 나더러 와서 동생의 여아를 학원3곳에  다녀주라고 하여서 택시를 타며 여러곳을 다녔다. 또 동생집에 갔더니 오래청소하지 않아서 지저분하였다.   3시간넘게 방청소,빨래를 하고 저녘밥을 지었다.  동생은 먼곳의 북경에서 일을 하고 있었고 집에 없었다. 동생집의  남자아이는 밥을 먹고 뒷방에 자기방에 들어가서 잠을 자고 새볔 1시반이 되어서도 동새여자의 핸드폰은꺼져있었고  새볔에 들어왔다. 안방에서 동생의여자가 딸을 때리는소리가 들렸다. 동생의여자는 딸을때리는것을 나더러 못챙견하게 하였고  나는 엄마한테 전화로 알려주었다. 뭔일인지 나는 모르고 있었다.  나는 동생네집에서 거실에서 TV를 보고 밤을 지내고 있었다. 어느날 또 하루 나를 불러서 동생집에 갔다. 그래서 갔더니 동생이 일을 다녀와서 집에 있었다. 동생은 자기가족들과 나를 데리고 식당에 가서 저녘밥을 먹고 동생집으로 갔다. 나는 또 거실에서 나의 오리털코트를 덮고 쏘파에 앉아서 티비를 보고 있었다. 동생은  안방에서 이불과 베게를 갖다주며 나더러 따뜻하게 잠을 자라고 한다. 그렇게 중국에 들어간 생활비가 없는 나에게 돈을 챙겨주며 먹는것을 챙겨주었다. 그리고  유아때부터 나의 딸에게 어린이날이면 공원에 데리고 다니고 학교운동회에 아빠의 책임을 하며 다니고 나의 딸을 챙겨주고 나를 도와주었다.  나의 동생은  마음이 착하고 
  다른사람을 해치지 않고 항상 도와주며 마음이 깊고 선량한 동생이였다. 아빠집에서 엄마는 동생이 잘먹는반찬들을 가득 만들어서 동생여자한테 챙겨주군 하였다. 하지만 동생집에  가서 보면 엄마가  만들어준 반찬들은 동생이 오면  절대 먹이지 않고 다른사람들한테 퍼주고 남은 반찬들은곰팽이가 생기도록 두었다가 음식물에 버린다. 동생이 집에 일을 다녀오는 날이면 나는 오랜만에 들어갔어니 동생이 잘먹는반찬들을  만들어서 갖다주면 동생여자는 싫어하고  반찬을 버린다. 어느날은 아침에 동생이 화장실에 있는 세탁기에서 쪼글쪼글한 옷을 꺼내서 입고 일을 나간다. 그것을 보고 나는 마음이 아팠다. 나의ㅈ동생은  반듯하게 다림을 한  옷을 못입고 따뜻하게 정성을 들여
  서  차린 밥이  아닌 배달음식을 먹고  대충 먹고   지내고 아이들을 위해 돈을 벌고 고되게 힘들게 처량하게 살고 있는것을 내가 중국에 들어가서 알게 되었다.  지모가 나의 오빠를  챙겨주고 그랬어면 오빠가 동생을 데리고 일을 하고  돈을 벌고 우리가족이 화목하였을텐데 우리 자녀들을 눈물나게  처참하게 살게 한 돌두 지모이였다.

  내가  첫결혼  딸을 임신했을때 여름에 옷가게 일을 다니는데 오빠의 집에 들리라고 하여  나는  퇴근길에   갔다. 오빠는 해외에 나가서 일을 하고 집에 없었고  형님은 살림을 알뜰하게 깨끗하게 하는 여자이였다. 형님은 내가 임신한거 알고 주방식탁의자에  앉아있어라고 하고 가루반죽을 하고 반찬통에 준비해둔 물만두속을 꺼내서 빠르게 만두를 빚어서 삶아서 한접시를 주었다. 시댁에서 얻어먹은것이 없고 받은것이 없는 나는 물만두를 맛있게 먹었다. 딸을 임신하고 먹은것은 그 물만두한접시밖에 없었다. 어느날 비가 너무 많이 내렸다. 그래서 시어머니한테 전화를 걸어서 옷가게에서 퇴근하는 나를 마중나오라고 시켰다. 퇴근하고 기차에서 내렸다. 철로길은 높지만 동네에 들어가는 길이 낮아서 물이 고여있었고  비는 계속 내렸다 . 철로길에 서서  물을 쳐다보고 기다려도 마중 나오지 않았다. 시어머니는 남편한테 연락을 주지않았다.  날이 어두어져서 어쩔수없이 동네에로 들어가는 사람들의 뒤를 붙잡고 임신7개월 몸으로 허리까지 물이 흐르는 세찬 물길을 더듬어가며 겨우 동네에로 들어갔다. 내생에 처음으로 홍수의 물길을 당하는길이였다. 집에 들어가니 집에는 바닥에 물이 들어가서 있었다. 바닥에 물을 퍼내고 정리를 하고 나서 잠깐 쉬고 있는데 연락을 하지 않은 시어머니는 와서 보지도 않고 남편은 마작을 놀다가 늦게 들어왔다. 그렇게 나는 딸을 임신기간에 일을 다니며  뒷밭야채밭을  가꾸며  석탄을 반죽하여 석탄벽돌들을 만들고 말리우고 창고에 가득채우고 겨울준비를 하고 집안일을 맡아서 하였다. 정씨네 집에서 시모가 싫어하는 나는 굶고  찬밥도 없는 신세로  지내고 어느날 찾아온 시모와 다투고 시모는 나를 쫓아내고 바구니에 울고 있는 딸을 놓고 나는 쫓겨나왔다. 나는 이혼하고  시모가 지모한테 던져준 딸을 키우며 고된 고생과 눈물로 외적들의 포위속에 절도갈취속에 치욕속에 이기며 나는 딸을 키우고 지냈다. 
  2004년 7월에 한국남편을 만나서 옷가게를 정리하고  2005년 3월에 한국에  입국하고 15년을 지낸 생활에 한국 남편은 나의 딸의 생활비와 교육비를 지원하였고 나의 부모를 초청해줘서 아빠가 골프장에서 일을 하며 고되게  벌은돈과 내가 준돈으로 아빠집을 작은 집을 사주었다.  또 한국남편은 나의 딸이 거주입주하여 생활할수 있게 은행에가서 대출하여   나의 이름으로된  나의 집을 사주었다. 그리고 나의 친모생모가 아닌 지모의 큰딸을 초청하여  한국에서 20년을 돈을 벌게 도와주었다. 나의 부모와 나의 딸의 모든생활비용을 먹고 살수 있게 한국남편이  지출비용돈들을   지원하여주었다. 한국남편덕에  나의 딸과 나의 부모는 생활비용을 겨우 유지하고 지냈다. 2018년북인에  9월에  강제강금 퇴원하었지만 그또한 외적들의 가해상해조작이였다.  나의 부모님이 데리러와서 중국에들어갔다. 2019년 이혼후 10월에 다시 한국에 입국하였다.  기습과 습격에 가해상해를당하고 병원치료비에 저축돈이 바닥이 나고 한국남편한테 치료비를 빌러서 병원치료를 하고 지내고 겨우 버티고 지내는 5년 세월에 여러번의 죽음에서 다시 깨여나고 기적같이 살아나고 내가 살았던 험악한 50여년  인생길을 글로 남기게 되었다.

  Of course I couldn't hope for spending this evening all alone with my sewing. 'Twas rather quiet and peaceful, as everybody had already gone to sleep, when Ginevra showed up. Breaking into my room, as if it was her own, she jumped right on my bed beside me with that wide and sly smile which*startled* me. Something has happened! However, Ginevra was lucky enough to catch me in a good posture. I was ready to listen to her *bemoaning*.
  'Why so happy and sly? Happened to flirt enough with someone?' I asked.
  I knew Ginevra well enough and her so-called ashamed facial expression only proved my guess.
  'Oh how dare you!' she exclaimed but her cheeks already gave her out showing this redness of joy and excitement.
  'Miss Holmes, your time is running out. I'm not going to pander to you this whole evening. Spit it out.'
  'You leave me no choice,mon ami! Oh, on this ball I met him!'
  'Him? What "him" are we talking about? The fifth one, with black mustache?' I was in very intrepid spirit, so I couldn't miss the chance to tease miss Ginevra Holmes, my "dearest friend".
  'You, cruel with these caustic remarks as always! No wonder your last name is Snider, miss Edith!' 
  But this bemoan didn't stop Ginevra from telling me about spate of holidays where she accidentally met Jean ( that was the nickname she gave him, so that no single soul will know her object of love) She, sometimes, even got into too much minutiae by telling how pleased, how polite and kind Jean was around her. How changed his demeanor as she entered the room. I hadn't interrupted Ginevra from her conceited and vain speech; I waited till the end, thinking about why on Earth I was chosen to be her confidante for we weren't joined at the hip, not at all. I opposed this since our first meeting, but Ginevra had this intrusive, clingy nature and I (God knows why) for some reason beared it.
  'Now you're done,Missy?' I demanded when she took a break, for she was talking quite fast, all fascinated by her own story. 'You never stop surprising me, miss Holmes! I dare say you're not even thinking about marriage, aren't you? It is just a silly game to you, a way to spend tiresome evening, am I right? I just keep wondering how this brave, determined and pure soul can exalt you. If only he knew your true motive, miss Ginevra! Childishness, boredom and delusion of grandeur! Here's my advice, miss Holmes, you better quit it if you have even tiny feeling of sorry for this man'
  'How difficult!' scoffed she at me ' I didn't get the half of the words you've said'
  'My speech was far from *abstruse*' I answered coldly.
  'So, you're convinced that my behavior hurts Jean's feelings? Well, I'm sure it doesn't.* Sue me*, bore! And nevertheless, I know that deep down even you would be pleased and entertained with this, prude!' 
  And Ginevra Holmes flew out of the room with cheerful giggle, leaving me alone in my room lighted with one single candle in the darkness of coming night.

      Русский ваш язык? Вот и отлично. Тогда переведите, пожалуйста, на английский фразу «мы своих не бросаем», а ещё лучше - «у нас своих бросать не принято». Получилось? Не получилось и не получится, потому что в «языке с самым огромным запасом слов» нет слова «свои» и противопоставления «свои - чужие», ровно как и слов «можно», «нельзя» и ещё массы других необходимых в обращении слов. Почитайте Булгакова или Достоевского на английском и почувствуйте разницу - перевод беднее в два раза, ощущение выхолощенности не покидает. Кстати, если почитать их даже, например, на французском, такого ощущения не возникает. Потому что он по всем статьям выразительнее английского и обладает бОльшим набором средств для выражения мысли. 
      Английский - наименее гибкий и многообразный язык из всех знакомых мне языков. Он чёткий, деловой, лаконичный - этого не отнять. Но богатым его не назовёшь. Слишком примитивно по многим показателям. А словарь его пополняется за счёт постоянных вливаний в него со всего мира, потому что он активно используется людьми во всем мире. Там полно неологизмов, терминов (в том числе куча терминов программирования, с аббревиатурами и цифрами которые тоже почему-то вошли в словарь!), интернет-словечек (однодневок) и пр. Но когда речь идёт о реальных словах языка, о его стандартной лексике - об этом я уже сказала выше.
      Поэтому ссылаться на сведения Гугла о том, что в английском языке миллион слов, что превышает количество слов в других языках - это ничуть не умнее, чем заявлять, что в арабском 12 миллионов слов. Но вам отчего-то мое заявление не понравилось (кстати, переведите заодно на английский слово «отчего-то»), да и намёк мой вы не поняли. Правда ведь (как по-английски «ведь» 🤔)?
      Полиглотам не мешало бы немного чувствовать языки прежде, чем о них рассуждать. А не слепо верить Гуглу.

      ​ @rogerteam5414  
      Not the person asked and it's been a month, but as a bored native English speaker....
      
      I've never met any adult native speakers who didn't know 'flabbergasted', but that might be a regional* thing. I would definitely not need a dictionary for that one.
      Quintessential is a bit trickier. It turns out I know what it means, but I just looked it up because I wasn't entirely sure if I was right or not. Most people would probably know it enough to get the point, but I'd imagine there'd be a fair number who would at least want to check with a dictionary if it mattered at all. I've seen college-age native speakers mix it up with 'essential', whatever you want to make of that.
      
      Regarding advanced vocabulary... both of these are words where if a native speaker didn't know them, it would seem a bit strange. I wouldn't necessarily think they're stupid, but they wouldn't come across as very well-educated. 
      On the other hand, if a non-native speaker knew these words, I'd be somewhat impressed. They're both fairly obscure and don't come up so often that I'd really expect someone who didn't grow up with the language to know them.
      
      One good thing, I suppose, about English being a second language for so many people is that most native speakers are at least sort of used to it. If your comment is an accurate reflection of your overall English vocabulary, then at least socially (and for a good number of jobs), you're at least good enough. 
      As a side note, using advanced vocabulary in social/most work contexts tends to make you seem like a pompous prick. It's a good thing to know for formal situations, but most native English speakers will (whether it's rude or not) use less advanced vocabulary if they know English isn't your first language, or at least not think too poorly of you if you don't understand.
      Overall, I'd say it's really not that much of a problem unless you want to be an editor for English publications.
      
      Being a native speaker would be speaking English as your first language. From what it sounds like you're saying here, that's unfortunately never going to apply to you. But with enough dedication, you can probably get to the point of sounding native in all but a few situations. Your English is pretty good already. It's good enough that if the conversation topic was different, the only way I might've guessed that you weren't native was that you wrote 'most of the times' instead of 'most of the time' (which is small enough that it also could also have been a typo).
      
      This ended up being much longer than I meant for it to be, but I hope something in here was at least a little helpful.
      
      *For regional context: I'm from the United States, more specifically the Midwest. I can't speak for the entirety of my region on these topics, much less the rest of my country or Anglosphere. 
      
      
      
      Other notes about the words you specifically asked about:
      
      'Flabbergasted' is a word I'd expect to hear, but it'd be a little weird to see it written. I suppose it might work in the dialogue of a novel, but otherwise it would (to me) seem a little odd. Not wrong, just odd.
      
      'Quintessential', on the other hand, is the exact opposite. Seeing it in semi-formal writing wouldn't seem out of place at all, but if someone said it during a regular conversation, it'd seem odd, bordering on pretentious. It might work in a business meeting, but even then it would usually be a bit much.

      Thank you for your comment. I agree that the paragraph about California is too similar to the original in its structure (in addition, I should have mentioned that a citation is needed to identify the source). It was a poor choice on my part, but I was just trying to get the basic concept across, that you have to focus on expressing the original meaning without focusing on changing the original word for word with synonyms. There is an explicit sentence in the video description that addresses this. 
      
      I would like to add that I made this video for my students, who are English learners, because they had a lot of trouble paraphrasing. Usually they would just plug in a few synonyms, and often the resulting sentence was unclear. I have another lesson coming soon that will explain more about the method of walking away from the original and using more changes to make it one's own writing.

  Great!  Tell me what difference can be found between summary and paraphrase.
    ↳ **@LearnAcademicEnglish [channel author]** (👍0 · 2022-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mF0mFwlnAY&lc=UgwN3f8s0e26BXnN4AZ4AaABAg.9Y56NNcSer-9Y6cdqSLcUw
      Good question! A summary is when you rewrite the main ideas in your own words. You focus on only the most important ideas of the original article. A paraphrase is a different skill because you can paraphrase anything --- any idea whether it's a main idea, a detail, just one sentence or a whole paragraph. You must use the skill of paraphrasing (writing in your own words) when you summarize. 
      
      I hope that makes sense! :)

      Hi Jean-Louis, I'm so glad that you found this video helpful! Paraphrasing is so challenging, even for native speakers. 
      Here are your sentences and some corrections and/or feedback from me: 
      
      1. Today in the world the majority of people who smokes lives in economically developing countries where as in former times they lived in richer countries.
      <The meaning is perfect. Here is my revision with a couple of grammar corrections:
      Today in the world, the majority of people who smoke live in developing countries, whereas in former times, they lived in richer countries.
      
      2. Students learning to expand their understanding of English grammar and vocabulary, will find that they will get better at paraphrasing. 
      <This one is correct, but take out the comma. We don't use a comma to separate the subject from the verb.
      
      3. First born children are inclined to be independent and successful to a greater extent than other children in their families.
      <This is correct. However, it might be better if you take out "to a greater extent" and add "more" before independent, like this:
      First born children are more inclined...
      
      4. The Covid-19 pandemic has increase the challenges faced by great numbers of people who suffers from underlining health conditions such as diabetes, heart diseases and obesity in the United States.
      <Very good. Add a -d to "increase" (has increased) and "suffer" should be singular (who suffer). 
      
      Thanks for sharing your answers!

      A figure of speech is when we use some words in a non-literal way. Here's the definition from the Longman dictionary: "a word or expression that is used in a different way from the normal meaning, to give you a picture in your mind" For example:
      He has a pea-sized brain. (meaning that it's very small)
      My dog just ate a horse. (meaning that the dog just ate a lot of food)

      Hi Sophia, You did a great job! I like how you moved parts of the sentence as one of the ways to make the sentences your own writing. 
      
      For #1, you wrote:  In this day and age, the majority who smokes live in poorer countries compared to in the past when the majority of those who smokes lived in richer countries. 
      
      Please notice my correction:
       In this day and age, the majority of people who smoke live in poorer countries compared to in the past when the majority of those who smoked lived in richer countries. 
      
      In #4, please use "who" instead of "whom" because it's the subject of the clause.
      
      Everything else looks great! :)

## Formal Writing — Smrt English
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s2gYq6KbhfA
- Video ID: s2gYq6KbhfA
- Views: 315 877 · comments total: 108 · engagement: 0.34 comments/1k views
- published 2012-11-15 · new comments in this batch: 93

**@AhmedAlaa-um8co** (👍39 · 2022-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s2gYq6KbhfA&lc=UgxXbUPrn3PWHyxNwM14AaABAg
  Be formal = use formal language
  
  Things to avoid :
  ----------------
  1) no contractions 
  - cant wont didn't
  - cannot , will not , did not
  
  2) No slangs or informal expressions
  -stuff , Awsome, ...etc.
  
  3) Avoid the use of the first person
  - I , me, my
  - So how to express yourself ? 
  
  - I think cellphones should be banned from classrooms ❌
  
  - cellphones should be banned from classrooms ✔️
  
  How -->The reader already know that you express your opinion "more objectivity"
  
  Why -->The reader should focus on your idea more than you 
  
  
  4) No personal examples 
  - experiences from your life
  - things and situations happend to your friends
  
  5) Avoid Addressing the reader directly
  - Dont use the word "you" too much
  
  Ex/ if you want to succeed , you should follow this process 
  -too causal 
  
  Ex/ following this process will increase one's chances for success
  
  6) No overly emotional language 
  - If the reader think you are emotional then you are being irrational ,therefore your argument is not valid 
  
  
  7) No over generalizations
  -the use of words like (every, none, All)
  Ex/ everybody knows that smartphones are useful 
  *Not fully true even if there is only one person who dont agree with that
  
  8) No statistics without proper reference 
  - Dont put a percentage in your essay unless you know where it came from "reference"
  
  Things to do instead :
  -------------------------------
  1) use the passive voice
  - impersonal , objective
  - it removes you from your ideas
  - quiet successful 
  
  Ex/ It is believed by some that the wide spread use of technology in daily life is affecting the way people interact with one another
  
  2) Use Academic vocabulary 
  - Bad --> Harmful , determintal
  - Help --> facilitate 
  
  💡When writing an essay make sure the language you are using is suitable For the task you have been given "Formal"

      @josephhorgan6543 
      Four key principles
      1.	Write the way you speak—the prime directive—then polish the draft message. 
      2.	Write for specific, busy readers—make sure the story interests them.
      3.	Think, write, and edit separately—they involve different parts of the brain and don’t mix well. Work with biology, not against it. Write a first draft with no edits.
      4.	Get to the point at the start—in sentences, paragraphs, and documents. Append secondary information to avoid clutter.
      
      
      Two key tools
      1.	Be concise at macro and micro levels—restate essential points and cut the rest. Use fewer words, shorter sentences, and shorter paragraphs.
      2.	Use active voice—does your document say who must do what? If not, it may use passive voice and hide the responsible party.
      
      
      Plus several supporting tools that I won't list here. One example:
      1.	Use pronouns, contractions, short transition words (still, also, so, but, thus, yet) and conversational style to improve and humanize the tone and reduce formality.
      
      
      We disagree on many writing concepts. For example, formal writing does not convey meaning well. It's sludge. Good writers avoid it: Darwin, Einstein, Adam Smith, Lincoln. Contractions are useful. Big words not so much. Maybe you use utilize and assist. I just use and help. The goal is to convey meaning clearly, so readers focus on that, without getting lost in confusing language.

  B2
  1. considerable
  1) A considerable amount of food produced is wasted; it's about one third of the food produced.
  
  2) There are considerable differences between a pro and an amateur.
  
  3) A: How could you make such considerable progress in English? B: I studied with Interactive English.
  
  4) His father had considerable influence over him.
  
  
  2. feedback
  1) Could you please give me some feedback after reading through all my work?
  
  2) A: Why does she look so depressed? B: She received negative feedback from her professor in her midterm.
  
  
  3. deeply
  1) John got into a car accident yesterday. He's in critical condition now, and I'm deeply worried about his health.
  
  2) Successful businessmen are always deeply concerned about their customers' satisfaction.
  
  3) The plan is deeply flawed. It doesn't make any sense at all.
  
  4) I feel deeply sorry for the mistake I made yesterday.

  6) Both of them are deeply in love. They are already engaged, and they are going to marry next September.
